articles.title_zh: China expels record number of officials from CCP
articles.content_orig:
China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering, which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平).
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.
Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25 percent of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.
The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia (張又俠), the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui (馬興瑞), the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society think tank, said in a post on X.
The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. However, in recent years the campaign has intensified, taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.
Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey.”
A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi and the military’s anti-graft czar, Zhang Shengmin (張升民).
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.
The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of next year. Xi is expected to secure a fourth term as leader of the party, making him the longest ruler of communist China since Mao Zedong (毛澤東).
The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo would be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

articles.title_orig: Intel stock plunges nearly 30%, on pace for its worst day since 1974
articles.title_zh: Intel stock plunges nearly 30%, on pace for its worst day since 1974
articles.content_orig:
Intel shares plummeted 29% on Friday and headed for their worst day since 1974 after the chipmaker issued weaker-than-expected guidance due to a plant shutdown in Israel and ongoing softness in the PC market.
The stock was on pace for its second-steepest drop on record. It's a major setback for CEO Lip-Bu Tan, who was hired in March 2025, and has since been on a campaign to revive the company after it missed out on the early years of the artificial intelligence boom.
Heading into Thursday's earnings report, Intel shares were up about 150% this year, buoyed by demand for central processors, which are becoming critical to agentic AI workloads. Analysts at D.A. Davidson downgraded the stock to neutral from buy on Friday in a report titled, "Not fixed yet."
"We understand the PC market is being impacted at the industry level," the analysts wrote. "However it is hard to justify the current multiple when weakness is so significant."
Amazon shares also sold off on Friday, slipping about 1%, after the company reported a third-quarter miss on the top and bottom line while maintaining its capital expenditure forecast for 2026 of $220 billion. Amazon also reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, and a big increase from the previous period.
The Nasdaq Composite slid more than 2.5%, capping off a week of rough tech earnings. Alphabet on Thursday suffered its worst day on record, plunging more than 12%. The stock fell again on Friday.
Other semiconductor names also notched declines. Chip giant Nvidia fell 4%, while Broadcom dropped about 6% and mobile chipmaker Qualcomm tumbled 12%.
Investors are growing nervous about the massive AI spending from the tech giants and whether their investments will pay off.
"I don't think this is a moment of reckoning but I think it's a moment where investors should take a long thought about how positioning across the space still remains crowded even though the fundamentals are strong," Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday.
For Intel, the disappointing forecast reflects a PC market that's getting hammered due to soaring costs for memory and other components. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier, according to Counterpoint Research .
Intel said it expects adjusted earnings per share of 25 cents this quarter on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts were expecting revenue of $17.1 billion and EPS of 43 cents, according to LSEG.
"We see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," Intel finance chief David Zinsner, said in the release. "We will continue making disciplined investments in capacity and working capital to increase supply and support future growth."
The guidance also accounts for the effects of an explosion at a fab in Israel that killed two workers and seriously injured a third earlier this month. The incident will cost the company about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters, Zinsner said.
Tan said the explosion, which he called an "unfortunate and tragic accident," caused an "extended shutdown" at the plant, impacting shipments of 10-nanometer chips.
Key to Tan's turnaround effort is Intel's foundry business, which has struggled to find its footing.
Intel is the only U.S.-based manufacturer of advanced logic chips, and is now in high-volume production of its most advanced 18A chip out of its new fab in Arizona, providing an alternative to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co . Its next Arizona fab is expected to begin operations by the end of 2028.
Intel still has no external customers for its new chips.
"We're going to have a couple of customers ready to announce the next two quarters," Tan said on the call, adding that Intel is making "tremendous progress" on its coming 14A chips.

articles.title_orig: US scraps G20 photo after European diplomats object to being pictured with Russia's Lavrov
articles.title_zh: US scraps G20 photo after European diplomats object to being pictured with Russia's Lavrov
articles.content_orig:
By WILL HALLOWELL, NEWS REPORTER and DAVID WILCOCK, DEPUTY POLITICAL EDITOR
Published: 10:57 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 12:04 EDT, 30 October 2026
A photo of diplomats from the world's 20 largest economies was reportedly scrapped after ministers refused to stand beside Russia 's Sergey Lavrov .
G20 officials, including envoys from Russia and China , are meeting in Atlanta, US, as they face deep rifts over multiple wars and other global crises that threaten international security and trade.
But plans for a group photo were axed after foreign ministers objected to being photographed with Mr Lavrov, Russia's top diplomat.
G20 participants even threatened to walk out of the summit if the photo op went ahead, according to US officials.
Already, a traditional family photo planned for Friday morning was called off shortly before the two-day meeting started.
Prior to these reports, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband had planned to boycott the 'family photo' and had asked for a separate photograph to be staged with close allies instead.
When asked on Tuesday whether he would shake hands with Mr Lavrov at the G20 summit, Mr Miliband, citing the war in Ukraine, replied: 'We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is chairing the gathering on Friday and Saturday that will set the stage for a G20 leaders ' summit hosted by Donald Trump at his Miami golf club in December.
Diplomats from the world's 20 largest economies reportedly refused to stand next to Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov (pictured) on 30 October
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, center rear, heads the opening plenary session of the G20 Foreign Ministers meeting on Friday
There appears to be little chance that the group will come to a consensus on many of the most contentious issues.
Among those are the Russia-Ukraine war, the US-Israeli war on Iran, US tariffs and Chinese machinations in the South China Sea.
All have contributed to spikes in the global cost of fuel as well as uncertainty about trade.
US officials say their top priority for the meeting is resolving differences over issues related to freedom of navigation, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the South China Sea.
The topic will include discussions on Iran, Russia-Ukraine and China and its smaller neighbors.
But hanging over the meeting is the prospect of new US military intervention in Iran, which has put the region, including G20 member Saudi Arabia, on edge.
US officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military strikes against Iran after Tuesday's midterm elections and the possibility that Iran will retaliate against them .
Some G20 countries have expressed concern that the US invited Russia, which will be represented in Atlanta by Mr Lavrov, during its heightened attacks on Ukraine.
Mr Miliband and Mr Lavrov are seated just feet apart at the G20 summit in Atlanta on Friday
China will be represented by a deputy foreign minister, but most other countries have sent their top diplomat, US officials say.
The US on Thursday scrapped plans for the family photo with G20 participants, according to two officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter.
The incident has endangered prospects for the world's largest economies to reach consensus on a number of global crises, especially the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
The US officials said Mr Rubio decided to cancel the photograph after determining that controversy over it would be a distraction.
It is unclear if Russian president Vladimir Putin will accept Mr Trump's invitation to the December summit in Florida .
US allies in Europe are uneasy with Russia's presence, especially after Mr Trump pushed ties with Ukraine to new lows by waiving fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limiting logistical and intelligence assistance.
Russia's foreign ministry complained of issues securing visas for its delegation that were only resolved at the last minute.
Those complications had created the impression that 'not everyone in Washington is happy' about Mr Lavrov attending, ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
But he would use the meeting to advocate for the 'swift reform of global economic institutions' and to promote Russia's vision of a 'multipolar world', she said.
Mr Lavrov has travelled very infrequently to Nato member states since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and the resulting severe sanctions were imposed on Moscow.
His presence in Atlanta is likely to cause both domestic political problems for Mr Trump just days before the midterm elections and roil at least the G20's Western participants, according to Ian Kelly, a US ambassador to Georgia during Mr Trump's first term.
'It seems politically boneheaded to invite him,' said Mr Kelly, who now teaches international relations and diplomacy at Northwestern University outside Chicago.
Mr Kelly noted that many Republican lawmakers, who are already fearful of losing their congressional majorities, are 'cranky' with Mr Trump's conciliatory approach to Mr Putin.
Democrats, he added, could use the invitation to bash the GOP ahead of Tuesday's vote.
In terms of the G20 itself, Mr Lavrov's attendance will almost certainly hurt efforts to produce a unified approach on the Russia-Ukraine war, Mr Kelly said.
'It will definitely take away from the message that at least the Western members want to send,' he said.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year as US officials said they made a conscious choice to only include formal members of the group.
Also missing from the Atlanta invitee list is South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group.
South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year , top US officials, including Mr Trump and Mr Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.
South Africa said on Friday its absence from the meetings was not voluntary.
'We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,' Phindile Kunene, spokesman for South African foreign minister Ronald Lamola.
Kunene welcomed support from other G20 members that had expressed reservations about the exclusion and said South Africa was ready to participate 'on an equal footing with other members' when Britain takes over the presidency next year.
The State Department said Rubio sees the event as a way 'to advance practical cooperation on shared economic and security challenges' and his priority is for the group to seek solutions to 'geopolitical crises contributing to global economic shocks'.
It pointed to threats to freedom of navigation, energy and food security and preserving supply chains of critical minerals.
However, there is scepticism that the G20 members will be able to overcome their substantial differences.
It will be less of a meeting and more of a test, said Elaine Dezenski, the head of the Center on Economic and Financial Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington think-tank that is hawkish on Iran and other issues.
'The Atlanta meeting takes place within an environment of widening disagreement over the global economic order, and the right test is whether the US can build cooperation with partners when all member consensus appears to be out of reach,' she said during a conference call with reporters.
She said the Trump administration had shown a willingness to work – and not insignificant success – outside the G20 framework to build coalitions that advance its foreign policy goals.
'The meeting offers a chance to assess whether the US can turn shared economic security concerns into more meaningful cooperation with partners even without the consensus,' she said.

articles.title_zh: Celebrate Warhammer Day with some suitably scary miniatures

Celebrate Warhammer Day with some suitably scary miniatures
Saturday is Warhammer Day ! It’s also Halloween, so, to get ready we’re taking a look at some of our favourite terrifying Warhammer miniatures.
Their whispered war cry is the last thing you’ll hear. These living suits of armour can’t be reasoned with, can’t be stopped, and they’re armed with magic guns!
Once proud Space Marines, Rubric Marines are now nothing more than a pile of dust and a corrupted soul, trapped inside a suit of power armour for all time, and commanded like a puppet by the arcane magic of warp-fuelled sorcerers. Some fates are worse than death.
What would Halloween be without vampires? Blood Angels may not dislike garlic, but they are incredibly stylish, and do crave the taste of blood. Just remember, Space Marines have two hearts, so you’d better bring two stakes!
Blood Angels have a second flaw – the Black Rage – and none have ever truly been able to overcome it. That was until Mephiston , Chief Librarian of the Blood Angels, crossed the Rubicon Primaris and seemingly left his curse behind him. Don’t think he won’t nibble your neck though.
While they may look skeletal, there’s no organic matter to be found on a Necron Warrior . These deathless automatons march without fear or mercy in eerie lockstep with a single-minded desire to destroy every living creature in the galaxy. You may be faster, but they’ll chase you forever.
Necron Warriors form the undead legions of the dynasties, and if it wasn’t scary enough staring into their dead, soulless eyes, then their guns can flay the flesh from any living creature. On top of that, one of their star gods was death incarnate, and is said to be the inspiration for the grim reaper .
The Nighthaunt are no mere ghosts, they are bitter, ethereal spirits that inflict terror, and drag down the souls of the living. Not to put too fine a point on it, these are not kids wearing bedsheets with eyeholes cut into them.
No figure in the worlds of Warhammer embodies the misery of the restless undead more than Lady Olynder, Mortarch of Grief . She is despair made manifest, gloom given form, and mortals in her presence are overwhelmed by a dread so potent that it can silence the heartbeat of even the strongest opponent.
While the motley assortment of creatures that make up the Gloomspite Gitz may seem “fun” to the casual observer, make no mistake, Squigs have very sharp teeth. And a lot of them.
When grots take to the battlefield with a horde of Squigs , woe betide anyone who underestimates these vicious creatures. Little more than mouths with legs and a terrible appetite, Squigs are feared across the Mortal Realms, able to tear even the mightiest foe to shreds in a crimson blur.
The full moon shines down through the inky black darkness. Out on the moor, you hear a blood-curdling howl. Wulfen are part Space Marine and part wolf, and they are probably the closest thing to a werewolf in the 41st Millennium.
Wulfen are bestial warriors, altered by the curse lying in the gene-seed of all scions of the Wolf King – hunters that bound forward with fangs bared and claws outstretched. They’re fast, and they hit hard with claws, teeth, and a variety of deadly weapons.
Join us in-store to celebrate Warhammer Day and Halloween! You’ll be able to pick up other scary models, such as skeletons , zombies , and other undead warriors . Plus, you can get Oath Fulfilled , the special commemorative miniature, who, if she gets sufficiently blessed by the Dark Gods, might make it onto this list for next year.

articles.title_orig: What next as Netanyahu's party claims Israel's election was stolen?
articles.title_zh: What next as Netanyahu's party claims Israel's election was stolen?
articles.content_orig:
Tel Aviv — Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party alleged Thursday that Israel's election earlier in the week was stolen by Arab-majority parties, helped by foreign funding that amounted to vote-buying, as final results showed Netanyahu's bloc has lost its majority in Israel's parliament, the Knesset.
Israel's Arab-majority parties had their highest turnout ever in Tuesday's election, winning an unprecedented 19 of the Knesset's 120 seats. Their success is one of the main reasons Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority and can't now form a new government.
The final election results show the far-right wing bloc's share of Knesset seats fell from 68 to 53.
Israel's Arab minority, also called Palestinian citizens of Israel, makes up about 20% of the country's population.
"Israel's elections have been stolen," Netanyahu's Likud party declared in a statement Thursday, claiming "an attack on democracy aimed at leading to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel, and the overthrow of the right-wing government to cause a withdrawal and defeat of the IDF (Israeli military) on all fronts — first and foremost, Iran."
The four parties that make up the main bloc opposing Netanyahu won 48 seats, so they would need some support from the Arab parties to try to form a coalition government, assuming none of the lawmakers currently aligned with Netanyahu's bloc defect.
The heads of Israel's two biggest Arab parties, which collectively won 19 seats, have said they would be willing to help the main opposition bloc oust Netanyahu from power.
Most of the Jewish-led parties that oppose Netanyahu vowed before the election not to rely on support from Arab parties to form a government, however, leaving a question mark over whether they might now be willing to cooperate to build a coalition to unseat the incumbent prime minister.
The Shin Bet, Israel's internal security agency, said it had opened an investigation into possible foreign influence in the election, but the scope of that investigation has not been made clear.
"An investigation of this type is also focused and bounded, and does not cast aspersions or place blame on an entire sector that went out to vote democratically and legally," the agency said in a Thursday statement.
The Acting Director-General of the Central Elections Committee, Din Livne, said in a letter to a committee member on Thursday that "there is no basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise of the integrity of the elections."
Israel media reports said one of the allegations the Shin Bet investigation would consider was whether Qatar had sent money to Arab parties in order to increase turnout among Arab Israeli voters.
Qatar's foreign ministry has denied the accusation.
"We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," ministry spokesperson Majid Al-Ansari said. "Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians."
While vote counting is now officially complete, the election results must still be certified and sent to President Issac Herzog before a new parliament can be sworn in and the process of forming a new government begins.
Gadi Eisenkot, head of the centrist Yashar party and the top candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, said he was worried that Netanyahu could be using the allegation of a stolen election to justify delaying or disqualifying the results.
"Netanyahu, who has accustomed himself to dealing with reality through lies, consciousness engineering, and the spreading of chaos, is leading alongside his partners an improper influence operation on the Israeli public aimed at delaying the publication of the election results on time and creating fictitious delegitimization of the activity of the 26th Knesset," Eisenkot said Thursday in a social media post.
Once the new Knesset is sworn in — even without a new government decided on —   Eisenkot's bloc, along with the Arab parties, could begin passing laws given that they will control a majority in the parliament.
Netanyahu, who President Trump endorsed enthusiastically , will remain in his post as a caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. If the parties cannot negotiate to form a new coalition government, then the country would have to hold the election all over again, and Netanyahu would remain the prime minister in the interim.

articles.title_orig: Treasury Department announces new Series I bond rate of 5.51% for the next six months
articles.title_zh: Treasury Department announces new Series I bond rate of 5.51% for the next six months
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury has announced new rates for Series I bonds.
Newly purchased I bonds will pay 5.51% annual interest from Nov. 1 through April 30, which is up from the 4.26% yield offered on purchases made through Oct. 31.
The new rate includes a variable portion of 4.08% based on inflation data , and a fixed portion of 1.40%. The fixed rate is up from 0.90% announced in April, and the highest since 2006.
Combined, the composite I bond rate is 5.51% after rounding, according to the Treasury.
Amid the post-pandemic inflation peak , the I bond rate hit a record high of 9.62% in May 2022, and investors poured millions into the government-backed, nearly risk-free asset.
As inflation cooled and I bond rates fell, many short-term investors redeemed I bonds . But investors could return as inflation pushes I bond rates back up, experts say.
"I bonds are a lot more attractive at this point," said David Enna, founder of Tipswatch.com, a website that tracks Treasury inflation-protected securities, or TIPS, and I bond rates .
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from an annual pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.
In September, some higher inflation came from the Iran war, which pushed up gasoline and energy costs . President Donald Trump 's tariffs, new artificial intelligence data centers and demand for travel have also added to rising prices , economists say.
Consumers expect rising inflation to continue. In September, the one-year inflation outlook jumped to 3.9%, the highest in more than three years, according to a New York Fed survey released in early October.
I bond rates have a variable and fixed rate portion , which the Treasury adjusts every six months, in May and November.
The variable rate is tied to inflation — using the consumer price index percentage change over six months — and stays the same for six months after you purchase, regardless of the Treasury's next update.
Your fixed rate doesn't change after purchasing I bonds. The Treasury doesn't disclose how it calculates fixed-rate adjustments, making it harder to predict.
Some experts believe the I bond fixed rate could be driven by real, or inflation-adjusted, yields from five-year TIPS, according to Ken Tumin, founder of DepositQuest.com, a blog that tracks I bond rates, among other deposit accounts.
"There's some uncertainty there," Tumin said.
If you currently own I bonds, rate updates follow a six-month timeline based on your original purchase date.
After you own I bonds for six months, the variable yield changes to the next announced rate. But the fixed rate stays the same for the entire time you own the asset.
For example, let's say you purchased I bonds in March when the variable rate was still 3.12% and the fixed rate was 0.9%. After six months, the variable portion would shift to 3.34%, announced in April 2026 , but your fixed rate would remain 0.9%.
You can earn I bond interest for up to 30 years, or less if you redeem the assets before that. However, you can't cash in I bonds for at least one year after you buy them. If you redeem within five years, you lose your last three months of interest.

articles.title_zh: ExxonMobil and Chevron report blowout profits as Trump touts benefits of high oil prices
articles.content_orig:
It’s a good time to be an oil company.
The two largest U.S. oil companies, ExxonMobil and Chevron, on Friday reported blowout profits that easily beat expectations as oil prices remain sharply elevated because of the U.S. war with Iran.
ExxonMobil reported a profit that doubled from the same period last year, while Chevron’s earnings surged more than 180% from a year earlier.
As part of the bumper returns, Exxon said it was increasing the dividend it pays to investors.
The returns at both companies came as the price of oil surged beyond $100 per barrel and has remained there for months. On Friday, prices accelerated again, with Brent oil trading just under $118 per barrel.
The highest level that Brent reached since the United States and Israel launched the Iran war in late February was $126, which it is now approaching again.
Since the start of the year, Exxon shares have risen 52%, and Chevron shares have returned 50%.
Overnight, another major oil company, BP, reported that its profit skyrocketed to an 18-year high.
The average price of regular gasoline has soared 40% for consumers since the war broke out. Soaring prices continue to pressure consumers ahead of the midterm elections, where voters have repeatedly said that prices and inflation are primary concerns.
In 2024, Donald Trump repeatedly pledged to drive energy costs down . “My plan will cut energy prices in half or more than that within 12 months of taking office,” the then-candidate said in September 2024, while adding that it would mean “gasoline below $2 a gallon.”
As of Friday, the average gasoline price is currently more than double that.
In recent rallies on the campaign trail, the president has celebrated the higher oil and gas profits. “I wonder if I should say this,” Trump mused aloud during a rally Oct. 24, before saying “our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happened in the Middle East.”
Trump touts U.S. oil business making ‘hundreds of billions’
“My people said, ‘Please don’t mention that, sir,’ because people are paying a little higher,” Trump continued. “But what we’ve done for this country, we’re making money like this country has never made before.”
“I don’t give a damn: I’m going to say it. We’re making a freaking fortune.”
The higher prices are also a result of the war between Ukraine and Russia following President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of his neighbor in 2022.
“There’s a lot of disruption happening in the world,” ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods told CNBC on Friday morning . “What you’re finding is because of the closure” in the Strait of Hormuz, “shipping has to find new routes around to continue to deliver the products that society desperately needs.”
“About half of Russia’s refinery capacity has been taken out from the Ukraine bombing,” he added.
“That shortage of refining capacity and availability to the world is what’s driving product prices as high as it is, and frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth,” Woods continued.
Since the start of the year, the average nationwide price for diesel fuel has risen 78%. New York-traded diesel futures have soared 130% since the start of the year, likely indicating more price rises could still come at the pump.
Both Exxon and Chevron said that they were running their refineries at maximum output to continue making as much diesel as possible.
Trump has taken specific note of the impact that diesel could have on the economy. The administration has quickly issued multiple orders and policies in an attempt to bring prices down.
The president signed an order allowing more widespread use of an off-road dyed variety of diesel, has pressured European allies to release more of the diesel reserves into the global market, and has announced a deal with Putin for some of that country’s diesel supplies.
Trump’s latest move came last week, when he announced $150 million in Defense Production Act funding to “expand petroleum production, storage, and logistics at refineries across.”
The moves have not meaningfully brought prices down.
On Friday, Woods said his refineries were already being pushed to the limit. “We are at record levels of utilization for our refineries,” he said on CNBC.
“If you look at North America, we produce record volumes of diesel. That’s all been a function of trying to drive more product into the marketplace to meet that demand and to drive costs down.”
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

Except until now, there’s been one Apple device not included in the app.
The Siri Remote for Apple TV 4K has historically been absent from Find My. There was another way to locate it using the Remote app via Control Center, but most users probably didn’t realize that feature existed.

It’s nice that Apple finally addressed this oversight, but the timing is no coincidence. That’s because the new Siri Remote (4th gen) is going to make finding a lost remote way easier.
The new remote features Precision Finding support and a built-in speaker . So the next time it’s lost somewhere in your house, your iPhone can direct you step-by-step to its location and trigger a noise to help.
The new Siri Remote is included with the 4th generation Apple TV 4K. But you can also buy it separately for $59 and get the same new features.
The upgraded remote is compatible with all Apple TV 4K and Apple TV HD models. To benefit from Precision Finding though, you’ll need an iPhone 17 or newer.

articles.title_orig: A Powerful Mosquito-Hunting Laser Uses A.I. to Zap Winged Pests
articles.title_zh: A Powerful Mosquito-Hunting Laser Uses A.I. to Zap Winged Pests
articles.content_orig:
For decades, humanity's answer to mosquitoes has been depressingly primitive. You slap your own skin, burn smelly coils, spray toxic chemicals that kill helpful bees, or hang up sticky traps that catch everything except the pests biting your ankles.
That manual era is ending. Companies in China have started mass-producing automated laser defense systems designed to track, target, and vaporize individual mosquitoes mid-air using artificial intelligence. It sounds like science fiction pulled straight from a military missile defense budget, but it's happening right now in consumer tech. Recently making news in related news: Why Microsoft And The White House Are Colliding Over Foreign Tech Talent .
The system, developed by firms like Photon Matrix Lab in Jiangsu province, doesn't rely on random zapping or chemical fog. Instead, it mimics high-end air defense architecture scaled down to destroy insects.
The hardware combines multiple tracking layers. Millimeter-wave radar and LiDAR sweep the room for movement, picking up the frantic wingbeat frequencies characteristic of mosquitoes. Once a target enters the perimeter, computer vision powered by artificial intelligence takes over. Algorithms calculate the insect's trajectory, velocity, and size in milliseconds. More insights into this topic are detailed by Gizmodo .
Then, a precision low-power laser fires a microsecond burst that instantly neutralizes the bug. It happens so fast you just hear a tiny pop while sitting on your couch.
This isn't the first time inventors tried using lasers against bugs. Intellectual Ventures famously built a mosquito-zapping laser prototype years ago using modified Blu-ray parts. But turning a garage physics experiment into an affordable, mass-produced consumer product required a massive leap in low-cost edge computing and optical tracking. That commercial breakthrough is what's driving the current production lines in China.
We keep throwing money at chemical sprays, yet vector-borne illnesses remain a massive global health crisis. Mosquitoes kill more humans annually than any other creature on Earth through diseases like malaria, dengue, and zika.
Chemical repellents like DEET work decently for a few hours, but they're messy, smell terrible, and wash off when you sweat. Indoor insecticide sprays build chemical resistance in local insect populations over time, forcing manufacturers to create stronger formulas that might not be great to breathe in yourself.
Outdoor bug zappers are basically indiscriminate slaughterhouses. They attract and fry thousands of harmless moths, beetles, and lightning bugs for every single mosquito they manage to catch.
An AI laser targets only the exact wingbeat signature of a pest. It ignores your cat walking across the room, ignores your kids playing board games, and ignores beneficial pollinators. It is precise mechanical elimination rather than environmental carpet bombing.
Before you throw away your bug spray, let's look at the practical drawbacks holding this tech back from total dominance.
Price is the obvious barrier. Early consumer vision-based bug locators, such as the Israeli-developed Bzigo Iris, launched at around three hundred dollars just to track and mark insects with a red dot. A full system capable of generating enough laser energy to actually kill a moving insect mid-air isn't going to be a cheap impulse buy on day one.
Safety is another major consideration. Even though these consumer lasers operate at low power levels designed strictly to damage insect wings or exoskeletons at short range, nobody wants a rogue laser beam bouncing off a glass table and into someone's eye. Regulatory agencies are going to scrutinize eye-safety certifications aggressively before these units land in living rooms across North America or Europe.
There's also the sheer volume problem. If you live near a swamp during peak rainy season, thousands of mosquitoes might swarm your porch every single hour. A single laser turret tracking bugs sequentially might get overwhelmed like an old computer trying to render a massive video game map.
We are watching a fundamental shift in how smart hardware handles household nuisances. Just as robotic vacuum cleaners took over floor maintenance by replacing brooms with algorithmic mapping, automated defense gadgets are poised to change pest control.
Laser defense units won't instantly replace bug spray or window screens. Instead, they will carve out a niche for high-end indoor protection in tropical regions or backyard patios where mosquitoes make outdoor living miserable.
As computer chips get cheaper and optical sensors improve, these systems will shrink in size and drop in price. The days of frantically swatting at shadows in your living room are numbered.
Elena Coleman is a prolific writer and researcher with expertise in digital media, emerging technologies, and social trends shaping the modern world.

articles.title_orig: Why Electronic Arts Shut Down BioWare And Cancelled ‘Mass Effect’
articles.title_zh: Why Electronic Arts Shut Down BioWare And Cancelled ‘Mass Effect’
articles.content_orig:
In his first interview since BioWare’s closure, Greg Zeschuk discusses EA’s acquisition, the leveraged buyout he calls the “final nail in the coffin,” and why great studios cannot be rebuilt with “random people and AI.”
BREAKING: BioWare Is Shutting Down
Greg Zeschuk was standing in the Babine River deep in northern British Columbia, fishing for steelhead when the studio died.
He didn’t find out until later that Wednesday, returning to the lodge, its sporadic cell connection, and a flurry of text messages.
BioWare, a studio he co-founded with Ray Muzyka and Augustine Yip in 1995 , which arguably went on to redefine the role-playing video game genre, launched some of the most respected games over its three decades, and helped earn Zeschuk and Muzyka the Order of Canada , was shuttered.
EA announced Oct. 21 that it was closing BioWare and ending early development on the next Mass Effect game . The closure cost about 50 jobs at the studio, part of roughly 400 layoffs across EA, and came 78 days after the company’s $55 billion buyout closed.
“I got like ten texts,” he said. “I came off the river and got to my little room and opened my phone, and it’s like, ‘I’m so sorry to hear about BioWare.’ And I’m like, ‘Oh sh*t.’”
He said by the time he flew home that Friday, he had “already shelved it away.” He also spoke with Muzyka, who declined, through Zeschuk, to speak with me for this story. Zeschuk said he turned down other interview requests while he was away; this is his first interview about the closure.
“I didn't have the immediate impact,” Zeschuk said, speaking with me from his home in Edmonton, where BioWare was also based, this week. “I wasn't there to share in the moment, which in some ways was nice because I was able to kind of just take my time with it.”
“I’m not saying it doesn’t hurt and doesn’t suck. And I think it’s kind of sad. It’s actually, in some ways, saddest for the city of Edmonton, where we’re from, because we were kind of this beacon of hope and excitement and possibility. We showed you could do something really special in a place that was not known for doing things like that.”
In a way Zeschuk already grieved the loss of BioWare 14 years ago when he and Muzyka both retired from the gaming industry in the same month.
“I've kind of gone through all the emotions like long, long ago,” he said. Leaving a company in a healthy way, he added, means breaking that emotional attachment. “You have to break from it and kind of go, ‘OK, I've had my emotional moment.’”
The real sadness with this news came from his concern about the people involved who lost their jobs and knowing how tough the games business is, he said.
“Anyone getting put into the job hunt is a sort of terrifying endeavor and super sad,” he said.
Some might believe that the writing was on the wall for BioWare when the founders sold the studio to Electronic Arts in 2007, but that’s not Zeschuk’s take.
In 2013, I chatted with Zeschuk about his decision to leave the company and pursue his love of craft beer. At the time, he talked about surviving EA.
“I think one of the reasons that we survived and succeeded within EA was that our company was mature enough and there was enough good people throughout to handle the EA bear hug – something that is well-meaning but vigorous,” he said at the time. “We needed to be strong to survive that, and I think we did, and you evolve from that as well."
This week, I brought up that bear hug again. Did BioWare ultimately succumb to it, I asked. Zeschuk said EA gave the studio several shots after he left, with Dragon Age: The Veilguard the last.
“They were able to operate within the framework, and they were able to put out products, I think,” he said. “And so that for me seems like it's a success.”
The first three shots happened, he said, “which is, I think, a pretty huge success.” The fourth, the next Mass Effect, never got its chance after the buyout.
He added that he doesn’t regret selling to EA, and he rejected the idea that BioWare sold because it was in trouble. “There was no coercion or pressure,” he said. “We were in good shape.”
“A lot of it had to do with the funding of the Star Wars project in Austin and just the stability of being in a bigger company,” he said. “I think at the end of the day, maybe we were ahead of the game a bit, but like we saw there'd be value in being part of something bigger rather than going our own way and taking all the risks.
“We had options actually. We thought we chose the best option that was available to us at the time. The company had good possibilities going forward, but at the end of the day we felt, OK, we may be better as part of a bigger thing.”
Zeschuk, like many founders in the game industry that I’ve interviewed, took a bit of a break from gaming when he first retired from the game industry. But these days, he says he loves playing games.
That said, he hasn’t played everything BioWare created since his departure.
“I played a bit of Anthem, but I didn’t play Andromeda,” he said. “I had a cooling-off period for a couple of years. Then I got back into it, and I’m a pretty avid player now.” As he’s gotten older, he said, he’s transitioned a bit away from story-driven games and more into what he calls “aggression-based” games. For instance, he said he’s played a ton of Nioh, Nioh 2, and Nioh 3, and enthused about completing the Underworld endgame mode in Nioh 2.
“I think I have over 1,200 hours in that,” he said. “I really like combat games. Maybe that’s where Jade Empire came from.”
He’s also a huge fan of Elden Ring, which he called probably the greatest game ever made. “Though the Zeldas are pretty close.”
I asked him if there’s a moment in time when he can look at BioWare and say that’s when the studio stopped being the thing that he and the other founders created. But he said a change like that at a studio is more of an evolution than a sudden switch.
“The way I look at that kind of stuff is studios are a function of the people, right?” he said. “As the people start leaving, it starts evolving and different people come in. I'm not going to have so much hubris to say Ray and I were the linchpin in the chain, our departure ruined everything. It wasn't that at all. I think we had a strong team with lots of people and there's lots of backup for things we brought and back up to the backup. But just over time, there's an evolution.”
He added that BioWare was always a very entrepreneurial kind of company, but that doesn’t really fit inside a bigger company.
“So I think it’s a slow and insidious kind of thing and again it’s the people. The people are the key.”
Zeschuk said that when he heard that EA was purchased in a $55 billion leveraged buyout led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund in August, he had an inkling things wouldn’t end well for BioWare.
“I think it was the final nail in the coffin,” he said. “I think that was the crux of it in a sense. Once again it's a completely different company now.”
And as a completely different company the new EA has a new set of priorities. While Zeschuk doesn’t have any inside knowledge, his suspicion is that the purchase was mostly about sports titles and “maybe Battlefield.”
“Everything else is kind of extraneous I suspect,” he said. “BioWare makes these kind of unusual games that take a long time and they're complicated and so it's easier just to pump out sports games every year and that's a better business model in some ways.”
Not everyone who reacted to the closure of BioWare has been as measured. Warren Spector, the now-retired designer behind Deus Ex and System Shock, called the closure “utter bulls**t” in a LinkedIn post , and said the executives involved should lose their jobs instead of the developers.
Zeschuk said he can understand that reaction. “Honestly, it’s not my rodeo,” he said. “I had to break with it emotionally 15 years ago…It’s so much healthier just to really, truly create that emotional break. Or else you’ll forever be second-guessing it a

articles.title_zh: 'Bad time to troll': Binance cofounder Changpeng Zhao asks Elon Musk for 'respect' after post about bitcoin hack
articles.content_orig:
The cofounder and former CEO of Binance asked Elon Musk not to "troll" the company on Friday and instead "show some support" after the SpaceX CEO appeared to mock the embattled cryptocurrency exchange in a series of social media posts.
After learning the world's largest crypto exchange had been hit by a $6.3 billion hack late Thursday, Musk posted several emojis, ranging from laughing to grimacing, on X.
In response, Changpeng Zhao reminded the SpaceX and Tesla CEO of Binance's equity stake in Musk's businesses.
Binance’s SpaceX stake, which stems from an earlier investment in what was then-Twitter, is worth more than $1 billion, Zhao said.
That's a tiny fraction of SpaceX's roughly $2 trillion valuation.
"Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop," Zhao wrote. "Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!"
It's not the first time the pair has sparred online.
In Nov. 2021, Binance suspended Dogecoin withdrawals because of a wallet glitch, a measure Musk called "shady". In reply, Zhao highlighted a major Tesla recall of almost 12,000 U.S. vehicles due to software glitches and hardware issues.
Binance froze all withdrawals and deposits after the hack, which investigators suspect to be the work of North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor. It has since restored deposits.
Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far.

articles.title_orig: Spain transport minister says he won't resign over high-speed rail disaster
articles.title_zh: Spain transport minister says he won't resign over high-speed rail disaster
articles.content_orig:
Spain's transport minister says he won't resign over the high-speed rail collision that has left at least 69 people dead.
Óscar Puente told a news conference in Madrid he had "nothing to hide" while repeating the government's vow to get to the bottom of the disaster, saying many questions needed to be answered.
"My duty right now is not to talk about whether I should remain in my position, but to resolve the problem," Puente said.
The transport minister has been facing calls to step down in the aftermath of the tragedy, including from political rivals, a trade union and demonstrators who protested outside the transport ministry on Wednesday night.
Dozens were killed and many more injured when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of another stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda, in the central Toledo province, on Wednesday morning.
A preliminary report released by transport investigators late on Thursday found the Renfe train was travelling between 160km/h (99.4mph) and 200km/h when the collision occurred, causing its front carriage to become embedded in the tail of the stationary train.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said earlier on Friday that public trust in Spain's high-speed rail network had been broken and repeated it was "unacceptable" that there had been two similar tragedies within a year.
In January a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people in Adamuz in southern Spain.
Wednesday's tragedy was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Puente said on Wednesday a computer failure at about 08:30 that morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the crash.
Three audio recordings between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Puente had said that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".
The leaking of the audio recordings has been criticised by some Spanish politicians, with Alberto Ibáñez, a member of Congress for the left-wing Sumar platform, writing on X that they were "despicable".
Meanwhile, Irene Montero - the prime ministerial candidate for the left-wing Podemos party - said responsibility for the crash should not be placed on one worker, adding that train drivers and experts have been warning against the liberalisation of the railway sector for years.
On Friday Puente said he was "not going to use any worker as a shield".
But he said "many questions" arose as a result of the tragedy and he wanted to look at them "one by one".
"If the investigation shows there is human error we will act in consequence of that," he said.
The conservative People's Party joined calls for Puente's resignation after trade union CSIF called for the same earlier this week.
But Puente said on Friday he would not budge from his position.
"The easy thing for me would be to leave, but neither that fits with my character nor is it what the Prime Minister has asked me to do," he said.
"I feel immense pain and immense sadness for the victims and their relatives... I cannot let this pain paralyse me though. We have to find solutions to this problem."
The country is observing three days of mourning, as the families of victims and the survivors of the crash struggle to comprehend how it could have happened.
A 24-year-old athlete and a former government minister are among the victims of Wednesday's disaster, but many families are still waiting for information from authorities about their loved ones.
Esther San Emeterio, whose 54-year-old brother Pepe is still missing, told reporters in Toledo, near Urda, that officials were forcing families to wait in "uncertainty".
"We went to bed crying, outraged and full of shame," she said. "We are desperate and I want all of Spain to know. How can they keep us like this?"

articles.title_orig: UK denies entry to Swedish academic due to speak at Palestine event
articles.title_zh: UK denies entry to Swedish academic due to speak at Palestine event
articles.content_orig:
London, United Kingdom – A pro-Palestine academic who was planning to travel to the United Kingdom has been denied entry because the government says his “presence in the UK is not considered to be conducive to the public good”.
The UK Home Office cancelled Swedish national Andreas Malm’s Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) on Wednesday, an email seen by Al Jazeera shows.
The decision came a week before Malm was due to appear on a panel organised by the British socialist magazine Tribune in London. Huda Ammori, cofounder of Palestine Action – which the UK has proscribed as a “terrorist” group – is also due to appear on the panel, which will be chaired by Hala Hanina of Palestine Deep Dive.
Malm, a climate activist and author who lectures at Lund University in Sweden, told Al Jazeera that he believes his ETA was cancelled because he was due to appear on the panel. He has contacted the Home Office for an explanation but is yet to receive a response.
“I have been going regularly to the UK for decades. My position on Palestine has always been public,” Malm said, adding that his latest visit to the country was in May.
“I haven’t said anything in public about Palestine during these intervening months or written anything about it. The only thing that could have caused this [latest UK decision] is that I was due to be on a panel on Wednesday evening, where I would talk to Huda Ammori of Palestine Action,” he said.
Malm used an ETA during his May visit to the UK, which allowed him to travel to the country again later in the year without seeking reauthorisation. He said he had received no indication from the Home Office that his ETA was at risk of being cancelled before receiving an email on Wednesday confirming that it had been revoked.
In its email, the Home Office told Malm that if he wishes to visit the UK, he needs to apply for a visa, after which the office will “consider your circumstances in more detail” before making a decision. However, the government website states that the processing time for a standard visitor visa is three weeks, meaning Malm would not receive it in time for next week’s panel even if his application were approved.
Travellers from countries whose nationals do not require a visa to visit the UK generally need an ETA. These include countries in Europe, the United States and Canada, among others.
The Home Office said it does not comment on individual cases.
“Decisions to refuse or cancel an ETA on the grounds that presence in the UK may not be conducive to public good are based solely on an assessment of the potential risk an individual may pose to UK society,” it said in a statement to Al Jazeera.
The cancellation of Malm’s ETA comes amid a wider crackdown on pro-Palestine activists by the UK government, something that began under then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
Tribune editor Oliver Eagleton said, “Andy Burnham’s government continues the authoritarian overreach we saw under Starmer. In this new dystopian Britain, it is now commonplace for authors and academics to be treated as terrorists because they support Palestinians facing genocide and the rights of people protesting that genocide.”
Starmer, a former human rights lawyer, was prime minister when the government proscribed Palestine Action last year.
The move classified the campaign group as a “terrorist” organisation under UK law, placing it on the same legal list as groups such as al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS). The proscription has been condemned by rights groups, including Amnesty International.
Most recently, Irish novelist Sally Rooney’s books were withdrawn from sale in the UK this month due to her public support for Palestine Action.
Rooney described Malm as a “brilliant and influential” intellectual.
“For the UK government to deny him entry to Britain is not only an outrageous attack on a respected climate expert, but a sad and frightening act of cultural self-harm,” she said.
Malm’s books include How to Blow Up a Pipeline: Learning to Fight in a World on Fire and The Destruction of Palestine Is the Destruction of the Earth.
Since Palestine Action was banned, more than 3,850 people have been arrested for publicly backing the group, in largely peaceful protests.
“This is a drift towards authoritarianism that didn’t begin with me and it’s not going to end with me either,” Malm told Al Jazeera. “If I’m now being deemed a threat to the public good because I’m supposed to have a conversation with someone from Palestine Action, this is guilt by association. Where does it stop?”
Gareth Dale, reader in political economy at Brunel University of London, told Al Jazeera that the Home Office’s decision suggests the UK government intends to continue suppressing free speech under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
“Andreas Malm is one of the world’s foremost campaigners on the two defining issues of our times – climate breakdown and the genocide in Palestine. Barring him from entry to the UK represents a monstrous attempt by the Burnham government to suppress free speech,” Dale said.
“Typical of bureaucratic tyranny, no reason was given for the ban; it is cynical and Kafkaesque. As Malm has committed no crime, we are left guessing as to the motives. Burnham cultivated the impression that his government would be turning a new leaf, but instead it is replicating Starmer-era authoritarianism.”

articles.title_orig: Did Apple and Amazon just save the smart display?
articles.title_zh: Did Apple and Amazon just save the smart display?
articles.content_orig:
Apple’s and Amazon’s new home devices might finally make the smart display genuinely useful. But they’re taking opposite approaches to get there.
Apple’s and Amazon’s new home devices might finally make the smart display genuinely useful. But they’re taking opposite approaches to get there.
Three years ago, I wrote an obituary for the smart display . The category — smart speakers with touchscreens attached — was stuck with a few underpowered gadgets from Google and Amazon that tried to do too much and did too little well. Back then, I also laid out what they needed to do to improve . This month, Apple and Amazon launched new smart displays that check nearly every box on that list.
Based on my brief hands-on time with Apple’s first smart display, the $299 HomeView , and Amazon’s $499.99 Echo Show 16, a ground-up rebuild of its smart display line, these could finally turn the smart display into what it should have been all along: the family computer. Not a place to do homework or pay the bills, but a shared screen the whole household can use to check the calendar, see who’s at the door, and figure out what’s for dinner.
The biggest shift is that both companies have finally brought computer-class hardware to the space: Apple with its A18 chip (the same as in the MacBook Neo ) and Liquid Retina display, and Amazon with a MediaTek processor and the same Nanomatte display as its new Alexa Tablet. This turns a category plagued by underpowered hardware and limited software into devices people might actually want to use .
The catch is price. In 2023, the Echo Show 5 cost $85 and the Nest Hub $99 . Apple’s HomeView, the cheaper of the two new models, costs three times that. But these devices now have a much clearer purpose, beyond being a vessel for each company’s revamped voice assistant . And with the software to back it up , they might actually be worth the investment.
As our lives have become increasingly digital, the need for a central place to corral all the information required to run a busy household has only grown. For years, the calendar, grocery list, meal plan, and chores all lived inside one person’s phone, creating an exhausting mental load. Add in the connected home, and the need for a communal device grows even greater: an interface anyone in the house can use to check who is at the door without opening it, adjust the thermostat, or dim all the lights with a tap or a quick voice command. Yes, some devices can do some of these things, but none do them all well.
The popularity of devices like the Skylight Calendar shows the need for a communal household screen. And while a tablet might seem like a natural fit, it has two challenges: limited multiuser support, and anything with a battery will wander into someone’s bedroom and die under a pillow. I learned that from personal experience. I thought Google’s Pixel Tablet, a hybrid tablet and smart display, was the category’s next evolution, though I wasn’t wild about its detachable screen. That turned out to be a big problem in my house — along with its half-baked smart home support. Google reportedly canceled its successor 18 months later.
With their new devices, Apple and Amazon are bringing three things to the category that I’ve been wanting for years: computer-class hardware, a display built for sharing that can easily switch between users, and a screen that is always on and as easy to use as a light switch. No PIN to enter or screensaver to swipe away, just reach out and tap to control your lights or scroll through your calendar. Both the HomeView and Echo Show 16 appear to solve these problems. (Of course, I’ll need to test them properly to be sure.)
Apple’s approach treats the person as the user; HomeView is designed to know you
However, that’s where the similarities end. What I find fascinating about these two side-by-side product launches is the different approach each company is taking to fit these devices into your household.
Amazon has built one screen for the household that works without your phone — you don’t even need one to set it up (although it helps). Apple has built a screen that is an extension of your phone; it has communal features, but they’re limited compared with what you can do if you connect your phone.
The reason for the split is obvious: Apple is built around the iPhone; Amazon is built around, well, everything else. Apple’s approach treats the person as the user; HomeView is designed to know you. In Apple’s demo, Siri AI knew exactly when your friend would arrive at the front door from the airport based on reading your text messages and could turn on the coffee machine so their espresso was ready the moment they walked in. But while HomeView has communal features, most of the good stuff seems to appear only when HomeView recognizes your face and your phone is nearby.
Amazon’s approach treats the household as the user; the Echo Show is designed to know your home
Amazon’s approach treats the household as the user; the Echo Show is designed to know your home. The company’s Omnisense technology built into its devices can sense presence, temperature, and room acoustics throughout your home. One of Amazon’s demos showed that when someone walks up your driveway, a figure appears on a map of your home , and you can tap it to see a live view of their approach through your Ring camera. While Amazon doesn’t have the same personal context as an iPhone, the Echo Show 16 offers broader features for the household, including meal planning, a full Fire TV, and a color-coded household calendar.
Amazon is selling a maximal feature set at a premium price designed for everyone while Apple is pushing a more polished, narrower product at a lower price, aimed squarely at its existing users. I’m looking forward to seeing which approach works best once I have these devices in my home. But for the first time in years, I’m excited about testing a smart display. I guess my obituary was premature.

articles.title_orig: Apple Is Entering Its Slop Era
articles.title_zh: Apple Is Entering Its Slop Era
articles.content_orig:
My ears perked up when I heard Apple’s new foldable phones were cracking . I licked my lips when the company announced it’s releasing a touch-screen laptop . This was a company that once charged $19 for a polishing cloth , asked $200 for a VESA mount , and sold $700 wheels for the Mac Pro. Now it’s borrowing tired ideas from its competitors and launching hardware its previous leaders rejected.
The once dominant company is struggling to find its feet in an AI-driven post-Tim Cook world. John Ternus is the new CEO — a 25 year veteran of the company with a track record of pushing harebrained hardware schemes like the much reviled Touch Bar and lawsuit inducing butterfly keyboard.
With Ternus at the helm, I feel there’s a good chance Apple’s best days are behind it, that it will have to make do with less, that it’s déclassé. Apple, blindsided by AI and relying on crowdpleasing hardware gimmicks, is downwardly mobile. It’s in its slop era. The company that once asked consumers to “Think Different” is now releasing hardware that’s just like everything else on the market.
Apple is not adjusting to this new position well. AI boosters agree that Siri AI is awful. Apple HomeView is a $300 Apple Watch meant to replace the family hearth . The iPhone Duo has only been out for a few days and all people can talk about is the cracks, yet Ternus is on the cover of Time Magazine this week holding the folding iPhone Duo and staring at the camera. “The other examples in the world felt kind of cheap and crappy,” Ternus told Time . Many people holding cracked iPhone Duos this week are learning just what (not) cheap and crappy looks like.
Flailing from crackgate, Apple announced the launch of a touch-screen laptop, an idea Steve Jobs extensively tested and said “doesn’t work ,” an idea Cook once compared to combining a toaster with a refrigerator . What’s next? What if the toaster-refigerator folded? Ternus has been trying to make an 18-inch foldable iPad happen for years . Maybe Apple will solve the screen cracking issues by then. Or maybe Ternus will continue to try to put a hat on a hat .
I have been waiting for this moment for more than a decade. I am relishing Apple’s recent trajectory more than I should. I confess I harbor a secret and petty grudge.
In 2010, when Apple released the iPhone 4 I was working as a floor manager at a Banana Republic in Dallas. I was interested in smart phones, of course, but Dallas is an expensive city and the iPhone was a luxury. I made do with my Motorola Razr . But the suit-wearing middle management retail psychopaths that were my coworkers saw my lack of an iPhone as a weakness. It was not, as they say now, On Brand.
I had started at the store in the stock room, working my way up to manage the backroom before ascending to a coveted position on the sales floor. The other managers made it clear that a Razr was a “backroom” phone and someone in a prominent position on the floor needed to be seen using an iPhone.
At first, I was not told to buy an iPhone. The message came in the form of subtle and not so subtle bullying deployed over weeks.
“Still using that old phone?” they’d say.“Didn’t you get a raise?” someone would ask a week later.
“Try not to use that thing on the sales floor,” one co-worker told me, pointing at my Razr. “We’re trying to project a certain image here.”
The social pressure had the opposite of its intended effect. I resisted. Eventually one of the friendlier managers pulled me aside. He told me that my colleagues thought it was weird that I didn't have an iPhone. He said I needed to buy one to fit in and he said the store could give me an advance on my paycheck to make it happen.
Ever the contrarian and pissed I was experiencing high school style bullying as a full grown adult, I threw in with Google instead. I got an HTC Dream . My coworkers weren’t happy, but they stopped bringing up the iPhone.
I’ve been an Android user ever since and studiously avoided Apple products until I broke down a few years ago and bought a Macbook Air. Time heals all wounds and Windows laptops are garbage. I’d even been considering changing from Android to iPhone because the privacy features are more robust. I’ve never been averse to a fast food meal either and maybe I’m a little more comfortable with Apple now that the cracks are starting to show in the foldable phone.

articles.title_orig: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
articles.title_zh: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
articles.content_orig:
China has rejected allegations of a Chinese espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, describing the claims as "groundless speculation".
US intelligence officials believe that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, was gathering information for Beijing on the US chip-making giant, according to a report by The New York Times .
The report said Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was under investigation over the possible diversion of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China and had developed a close relationship with Jensen.
Nvidia told the paper their interactions were routine business engagements, while Beijing accused Washington of attempting to smear China. Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.
The BBC has contacted Nvidia and Megaspeed for comment.
US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.
Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".
It remains unclear what information Alice Huang - who is also known as Huang Le - allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.
At a regular briefing on Friday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said: "The report in question is based on groundless speculation and is nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
The paper's report comes amid longstanding US concerns about China's access to advanced computing technology, which is considered crucial to developing artificial intelligence systems.
Jensen Huang has argued that allowing Nvidia to sell more of its products to China is important for maintaining US competitiveness in the global AI industry.
But Washington has restricted exports of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China since 2022, citing national security concerns and the risk that the technology could strengthen China's military operations. There have however been some loosening of restrictions during Trump's administration.
US officials said they had caught several firms illegally trafficking the chips across the Chinese border. They have also investigated whether companies operating through third countries are helping Chinese businesses access the restricted technology.
Nvidia has said it complies with applicable export laws and that there is no evidence its chips have been smuggled into China.
In response to the allegations made by the Times, John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, told the paper: "Jensen's interactions with Ms Huang are not unusual or unexpected".
He said customers like Megaspeed "receive ordinary business information - not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets - and zero information relevant to national security."
He added that allegations the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China "were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year".
Megaspeed said its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. The company also said it had informed the US government that it was willing to cooperate.
It is unclear how closely Alice Huang remains involved with Megaspeed.

articles.title_orig: The Clever 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid Feels Like An EV, But Never Needs Plugging In To Get 530 Miles Of Range
articles.title_zh: The Clever 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid Feels Like An EV, But Never Needs Plugging In To Get 530 Miles Of Range
articles.content_orig:
As drivers get squeezed at the pump due to high gas prices, they’re increasingly seeking cars that can go farther on a tank of gas, leading to record sales of hybrids for Toyota, Honda, Hyundai, and Kia this year.
Nissan, however, has been notably absent from this party, with no plug-less hybrid in its U.S. lineup. The 2027 Rogue Hybrid finally changes that, and it will lock horns with rivals such as the Toyota RAV4, Honda CR-V Hybrid, and Hyundai Tucson Hybrid. But does it have what it takes to challenge these more established names in this segment?
I drove the new Rogue last week and came away impressed. Its unique powertrain makes the gas engine work solely as a generator to charge the battery. The engine has no mechanical connection to the wheels, which are driven by electric motors the whole time.
As a result, the Rogue drives like an EV with impeccable refinement and smoothness. I drove it back to back with the RAV4, and the Rogue felt superior with its EV-like traits. The RAV4 outperforms in some other areas, but the Rogue is particularly strong when it comes to driving characteristics. Let’s dive right in.
[ Full Disclosure: Nissan invited me to drive the 2027 Rogue Hybrid in Santa Barbara, California. It paid for travel, accommodation, and food.]
Don’t let anyone fool you into thinking that hybrids are new. They’re older than the iPhone. The Toyota Prius made its U.S. debut in 2000, and while hybrid technology has incrementally improved since with efficiency and performance gains, the basic formula is unchanged: pair a gas engine with one or more electric motors and a small battery for better fuel economy.
Nissan’s e-Power hybrid system isn’t new, either. The automaker has sold nearly 2 million vehicles equipped with the technology worldwide since 2016, but it’s bringing it to the U.S. only now.
So why the wait? Nissan executives said the first two generations of e-Power were designed for markets such as Japan and Europe, where smaller, front-wheel-drive vehicles are more common. The Rogue Hybrid’s third-generation e-Power system, with a more powerful, dual-motor all-wheel-drive setup, is tailored to North American driving conditions. It was developed for higher speeds and American drivers’ performance needs, Nissan said.
The 5-in-1 electric drive unit combines the reducer, inverter, increaser, motor, and generator. It's showcased here within the broader 1.5 liter engine assembly.
The Rogue, however, feels refreshingly different from rivals. It is powered by a 1.5 liter, three-cylinder turbocharged gasoline engine which shares no components with the power plant on the current Rogue, according to the company. The engine is paired to a 1.67 kilowatt-hour lithium ion battery, which powers two permanent magnet motors, one on each axle.
It is designed to run in its most efficient power band around 2,000 rpm for regular driving but it can rev up to 5,500 rpm under extra load. The generator converts the engine’s mechanical rotation into electricity, whereas the inverter handles alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) conversion for the high-voltage battery and back to AC for the e-motors. With no direct mechanical linkage between the engine and the wheels, or between the front and rear axles, the electric motors do all of the driving.
That’s the primary distinction between this system and the ones that power Toyota and Honda hybrids. Engines in those hybrid systems are also connected to the wheels, and they use an electronic-continuously variable transmission (e-CVT). There’s no traditional transmission on the Rogue hybrid, just direct drive to the electric motors via the battery.
2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid Specifications
Pulling out of the parking lot, I could barely tell the Rogue’s engine was running. Around town, the SUV is quiet and smooth, with the combustion engine largely imperceptible. It was only once I hit the freeway that I began to hear a faint, distant rumble. There’s no instant torque like an EV, no turbo lag like a combustion engine, nor any flat acceleration like a traditional hybrid—just a smooth, consistent, and progressive power delivery.
Hopping into the RAV4 back to back made the Rogue Hybrid’s strengths even more clear. Under acceleration, the RAV4 produces that coarse and unpleasant rubber band effect from its e-CVT. With no transmission, the Rogue makes no such noises. It’s plenty quick, too, hitting 60 miles per hour in 6.4 seconds, which Nissan said makes it the fastest accelerating SUV in the segment. However, the build up of speed is more effortless than jarring—you’re not going to scare your passengers away when you floor the throttle.
It also gets one-pedal driving and recovers energy from braking for better efficiency. One pedal driving worked as advertised, although it didn’t slow down the vehicle as quickly as an EV. I found myself having to lift off the accelerator earlier than I would have liked to give it enough room to stop before a crosswalk or a stop sign. Until you learn to anticipate its braking behavior, you’ll find yourself reaching for the brake pedal more often than you would in an EV with stronger regenerative braking.
The Rogue also gets what Nissan calls “Smooth Stop.” It basically avoids head toss when the SUV fully stops, something we’ve also experienced in the BMW iX3 . It does this by precisely controlling the brake force moments before the vehicle stops, factoring in things like gradient and speed, to avoid your head from bobbing forward and back. It will also sense your foot’s pressure on the pedal. If you’re feathering the brake or pressing hard, head toss is controlled regardless. It’s a small feature, but can make stop-and-go traffic feel less tiring.
The Rogue Hybrid delivers an EPA-rated city/highway/combined fuel economy of 41/36/38 miles per gallon. All of that is better than the non-hybrid third-generation Rogue currently on sale, which is rated for just 30 mpg combined and less than that on most trims. The RAV4 is more efficient, with an EPA rated city/highway/combined fuel economy of 46/39/42 mpg. In my testing earlier this year, I observed 47 mpg combined and up to 56 mpg in the city with the Toyota. So the RAV4 is both more efficient in the city and on the highway, but the Rogue Hybrid doesn't appear to be far behind. (The fuel economy varies slightly depending on trims.)
The suspension also felt sophisticated on the new Rogue. The ride around town was supple, with the springs absorbing the bumps really well and minimal jolts filtering into the cabin. The SUV doesn’t thud or crash over large expansion joints and feels planted at highway speeds. The excellent ride, plus the EV-like refinement and smooth acceleration makes it feel like a premium SUV belonging to a segment above.
While Nissan seems to have gone all-in on making the driving experience great, the same effort doesn’t quite extend to the cabin.
The seats are soft and comfortable, but the interior lacks a cohesive design language. The center console, in particular, feels like an afterthought, with square, plasticky gear selector buttons and climate controls that look out of place. At least they work well, and I’m glad Nissan hasn’t succumbed to the trend of burying basic functions in touchscreen menus.
The dual 14.3-inch displays looked crisp, and the central touchscreen felt slick and responsive, although my limited time with the vehicle didn’t allow for a more comprehensive review of the infotainment. Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto come standard, while the top-spec Platinum trim adds Google built-in with Gemini and a 10-speaker Bose audio system.
There are some thoughtful touches, too. The wireless phone charger is MagSafe-compatible, so your iPhone won’t rattle. The rear doors open to nearly 90 degrees, so you have more room while installing child seats and easier ingress and egress.
