articles.title_orig: Lenovo Googlebook 15 Review: Your Android Phone's New Best Friend
articles.title_zh: Lenovo Googlebook 15 Review: Your Android Phone's New Best Friend
articles.content_orig:
Googlebook's clumsy launch made me wish that I wasn't a product reviewer. I had to spend two weeks using a laptop with what felt like an unfinished operating system (cue the world's smallest violin), and throughout the entire process, I just kept thinking how nice it would be if Google had taken all of its biggest Googlebook features and slapped them on a mainline Linux distro instead of trying to reinvent the wheel.
Anyways, I tried to replicate these features on an old Surface Go that I bought for about $60 and loaded up with CachyOS, mainly because I thought it would be funny to do so, but also to demonstrate that you don't need to drop $800+ on a Googlebook to get some of its key functionality.
If you've never tried KDE Connect, go install it now. Not only does it enable texting from your Linux, Windows, or macOS desktop, but it lets you sync Android notifications to your PC, transfer files between your devices, and sync your clipboards. You can even use KDE Connect to control your PC from your phone , which feels like witchcraft, although it's arguably the least useful of these features.
Best of all, KDE Connect operates within your local Wi-Fi network, so it doesn't rely on external Google servers to sync your clipboard or notifications. You aren't restricted in which devices you connect, either. I've got several Android phones at my desk, plus an iPhone and Mac, and I can connect them all to my Linux laptop at once through KDE Connect if I want to.
GooglebookOS treats basic Android phone integration as a major selling point, which feels a bit odd to me, as KDE Connect and similar tools (including the official Microsoft Phone Link utility ) have been around for years. Plus, the Googlebook's Android integration is fairly broken at launch. I couldn't get basic features like Quick Share file transfers working at all when I reviewed the ASUS Googlebook 14 .
Though I will admit that the KDE Connect interface is kind of ugly. The good news is that Google Messages is available on the web, so I can just access it through my Linux laptop's browser if I want a prettier texting experience. There are also some file transfer tools with more attractive frontends than KDE Connect, such as Packet .
One of Googlebook's headline features—screen mirroring—didn't really work for myself, my colleagues, or too many other people at launch. It might still be kind of busted when this article goes live, for all I know.
Anyways, setting up Android phone mirroring in Linux took all but five minutes and worked without a hitch, all I had to do was install scrcpy , connect my Android phone to the laptop with a USB cable (after enabling USB debugging in Android's developer settings), and punch the scrcpy command into my terminal.
Not only does scrcpy mirror your Android phone's screen to your Linux desktop, but it lets you interact with the screen using your mouse and keyboard, just like how Googlebook phone mirroring is supposed to work. You can even use autoadb to automatically fire up scrcpy when you connect your phone to your PC, but I didn't bother, as I actually prefer the manual startup behavior.
To be honest, I was pretty delighted to see this working on my pathetic little Surface Go, which uses a Pentium 4415Y processor. But scrcpy's wireless mode, which you can trigger through the scrcpy --tcpip command (run the command while your phone is plugged in, then unplug it) didn't seem to be particularly fond of my Surface Go's Wi-Fi capabilities, and setting up wireless mirroring without a USB cable is somewhat cumbersome, so I guess scrcpy loses points there.
Is smartphone mirroring actually useful? To be perfectly honest, I haven't found any use for it beyond watching TikToks while reading emails on my Mac. But screen mirroring is a landmark Googlebook feature that didn't work for me or my colleagues at launch , so I had to replicate it in Linux out of spite.
Some of the Googlebook's Gemini integrations feel a bit lazy or clunky , but Magic Pointer is surprisingly polished. It's a desktop-based take on Android's "Circle to Search" feature: wiggle your cursor and highlight something on screen to show it to Gemini. The AI will explain what you're looking at or provide suggestions without pulling up a full chat window.
I managed to find some tools that loosely replicate Magic Pointer functionality. The best looking option is AIPointer , a tool that lets you select an area on your screen and send it to your LLM of choice. You can even use AIPointer to instantly send up to five files to an LLM, which sounds pretty handy to me.
The problem is that AIPointer and similar tools require an API key. And after spending a few weeks with a Googlebook, I've come to the conclusion that I don't use Magic Pointer enough to justify paying for it.
So, I've come up with a free solution—I can just take a screenshot and drag it into a ChatGPT or Claude window. If I need to ask an LLM about something on my screen, then it's probably going to require a conversation with some back-and-forth anyway, so it's not like I'm "wasting time" by opening a full chat.
This solution does lack some of Magic Pointer's automation features, such as the ability to add a date to your calendar by wiggling your cursor and pointing at it. But there are browser extensions like Text to Google Calendar that offer similar functionality, so I'm not too stressed about it.
Googlebook OS is built on Android's desktop interface, so naturally, it runs Android apps. It's a neat idea at a conceptual level, and it's something that's got a lot of potential if developers put their best foot forward, but it's pretty clunky at launch.
A lot of apps simply aren't available on the Googlebook Play Store, while others aren't optimized for the desktop at all. Plus, essential apps like Chrome currently lack key features that have been supported on Linux, Windows, and macOS for years.
Anyway, I tried replicating this functionality with Waydroid , which is a containerized utility that lets you run a full Android operating system on your PC. It even lets you go into multi-window mode so that each app is treated like a standalone window on your desktop.
But I quickly gave up on trying to replicate this Googlebook feature because it just isn't worth it on my poor, weak little Surface Go. There are visual bugs that I don't feel like putting in the effort to fix, and the performance is just generally rough. Nevermind the tedium of grabbing apps and setting up networking, which are just too time consuming, seeing as I'll probably never open Waydroid on my Surface Go again.
This is an area where the Googlebook obviously has a huge leg up. Whether Android apps are actually worth running on desktop is a matter of opinion, of course.
My favorite Googlebook feature, which is also available on Pixel 11, is the Rambler speech-to-text processor . I'll admit that this feature is somewhat niche, but it's the best speech-to-text tool I've used to date.
There are plenty of tools that accomplish Rambler-like functionality, most of which are based on OpenAI's Whisper model (which works offline and doesn't require API credits). Unfortunately, my poor Surface Go's Pentium 4415Y processor is way too weak for this level of realtime transcription. I gave the OpenWhispr and Handy frontends a go just to see what would happen, and my Surface Go threw up an overheating screen. Oops!
I can probably get around this issue by using a text-to-speech tool on my Android phone, copying the output to its clipboard, and syncing the clipboard to my Surface Go through KDE Connect. But there's not much utility in that outside of long-form writing since it's a bit tedious.

Scottish police are investigating the time convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein spent with Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor at Balmoral, a private royal estate in Scotland which is a favored retreat for the monarchy.
“We have received information and active enquiries are ongoing but these are at a very early stage,” a Police Scotland spokesperson told CNN on Friday, without giving details about the investigation.
“All enquiries are evidence-led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those enquiries,” the police spokesperson said. “We would never confirm details of ongoing enquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further.”
British newspaper The Daily Express reported that the investigation was related to allegations women were “trafficked” to Balmoral.
Since the release of the Epstein files, Mountbatten-Windsor, known as Prince Andrew until his brother King Charles III stripped him of his titles, has faced a slew of allegations over his links to the late sex offender. He was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office in February and interviewed under caution before being released.
The scandal has left Mountbatten-Windsor’s already battered reputation in tatters and plunged Britain’s royal family into crisis.
Pictures previously released by US prosecutors in 2021 appear to show Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell, the financier’s right-hand woman currently serving time in a US federal prison for sex trafficking and other crimes, at Balmoral in 1999.
Buckingham Palace has consistently said that it does not speak for Mountbatten-Windsor and does not comment on active police investigations.
Mountbatten-Windsor has vehemently denied any and all wrongdoing in his dealings with Epstein. Police have said their investigation into misconduct in public office, relating to his time as a trade envoy for Britain, is still ongoing.
CNN’s Sharon Braithwaite contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
articles.title_zh: Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
articles.content_orig:
Novaya Gazeta, Russia's last independent newspaper, announced Friday that it will cease operations from Nov. 9, marking a major milestone for President Vladimir Putin's years-long effort to silence the country's free press.
Novaya Gazeta said it was being forced to close under pressure from Russian authorities and security services.
"The newspaper no longer exists," editor in chief Sergei Sokolov said in a video statement shared Friday on YouTube . "The Russian government, Russian special services, forced the editorial team to stop its work."
The announcement came a day after the newspaper's staff learned they were being evicted from their Moscow newsroom on Potapovsky Lane, where journalists had worked for nearly 30 years. At the same time, the system that enabled readers to donate to the paper was switched off, cutting its only remaining source of funding.
The Anna Politkovskaya Museum, a memorial to the paper's renowned investigative journalist who was shot dead two decades ago, will close with the newspaper, as it has been housed in her former office.
Sokolov said authorities had left the team no choice but closure. In his statement he said the newspaper's staff would now "end on the street, with no means of subsistence and under the constant threat of repression."
Novaya Gazeta was founded in 1993 with money donated by former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, from his Nobel Peace Prize award. It became the standard-bearer for investigative reporting in post-Soviet Russia, exposing corruption and human rights abuses, including Politkovskaya's reporting on the war in Chechnya.
She was gunned down in Moscow in 2006, becoming one of multiple journalists killed over the years in allegedly politically motivated assassinations , including at least two others who were with Novaya Gazeta. Politkovskaya's convicted murderer was pardoned by Russian authorities in 2023 after he joined the military to fight in Ukraine.
In 2021, the newspaper's then-editor Dmitry Muratov was jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize , along with Philippine journalist Maria Ressa, for defending freedom of expression.
Shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Novaya Gazeta suspended its print and online operations following repeated warnings from Russia's state media regulator about violating laws on alleged "false information," and a court stripped the outlet of its media license that September.
With the closure of Novaya Gazeta on Friday, there are now no major independent newspapers still operating inside Russia.
Independent radio station Ekho Moskvy and the TV Rain network had already shut down operations inside Russia under similar pressure from authorities. Some Novaya Gazeta staff left Russia and launched a sister outlet in Europe, which Russian authorities have also blocked access to inside the country.
Katya Kotrikadze, news director for TV Rain, which now operates in exile from Europe and is not accessible in Russia, told CBS News on Friday that Novaya Gazeta's closure did not come as a surprise.
"There was no freedom of speech and media in Russia for years now, it has been destroyed for years now," she said, adding that Novaya Gazeta had not been able to objectively cover the war in Ukraine due to censorship that was tightened at the start of the full-scale invasion.
Putin "has burned all the bridges and has stopped all the imitation of democracy and freedom of everything in Russia," she said.
Novaya Gazeta said it would provide more information about its future in the coming days.

Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev will not attend Friday’s Organization of Turkic States (OTS) summit in Ankara, Azerbaijani media reported Thursday, amid tensions between the two close allies over Turkey’s criticism of restrictions on headscarves in Azerbaijani schools.
Aliyev will be represented by Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov at the October 30 summit, according to the Azerbaijani Report Information Agency , which attributed his absence to previously scheduled engagements and a busy work schedule.
The agency reported that Aliyev would attend the final and closing ceremony of the inaugural FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival in Baku on Friday and present awards to the finalists. It said his participation in the ceremony had been arranged in advance.
The announcement comes despite Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s personal invitation to Aliyev during an October 21 telephone conversation and the departure of Erdoğan’s chief presidential adviser, Oktay Saral, following a dispute over Azerbaijan’s restrictions on headscarves in schools.
Saral criticized the restrictions in an October 12 post on X, saying it was unacceptable to prevent students wearing headscarves from exercising their right to education.
Azerbaijan amended its school uniform regulations in September to prohibit clothing considered inconsistent with prescribed uniforms or secular education. Although the regulations do not explicitly mention headscarves, some students wearing them have reportedly been turned away from classes.
Saral’s remarks prompted a sharp response from Azerbaijan’s ruling New Azerbaijan Party, which accused Turkish political figures of interfering in the country’s domestic affairs.
In an October 25 interview with journalist Talat Atilla, Saral said he was leaving his position on Erdoğan’s instructions. Asked whether his departure was connected to his criticism of Azerbaijan, he replied, “Yes, it seems so.”
Saral announced his resignation the following day.
Middle East Eye had reported that Azerbaijan demanded Saral’s dismissal and legal action against Turkish commentators accused of insulting Aliyev.
The dispute has also resulted in measures against Turkish citizens. Azerbaijan has barred 31 Turkish nationals, including journalists, political figures and religious commentators, from entering the country and issued arrest warrants for seven others over statements related to the controversy.
Tensions between Ankara and Baku predate the headscarf controversy, Azerbaijani political analyst Arastun Orujlu told Meydan TV, an independent Azerbaijani news outlet operating in exile.
He identified Azerbaijan’s increasingly close ties with Israel as a major source of friction, pointing to broader competition between Turkey and Israel for influence in the South Caucasus.
Despite the tensions, Aliyev sent Erdoğan a message Thursday congratulating Turkey on the 103rd anniversary of the founding of the republic.
He described Azerbaijan and Turkey as bound by genuine ties of friendship and brotherhood and said the 2021 Shusha Declaration had elevated their relationship to the level of an alliance.
The announcement of his absence from the summit came later that day.
Bayramov, who will represent Azerbaijan at the summit, attended Thursday’s meeting of the OTS Council of Foreign Ministers in Ankara and met with his Turkish counterpart, Hakan Fidan.
The ministers discussed bilateral relations and regional and international developments, according to the Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry.
Friday’s summit, hosted by Erdoğan, will mark Turkey’s taking over the organization’s rotating chairmanship from Azerbaijan.
The OTS, which brings together Turkey, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, promotes political, economic and cultural cooperation among Turkic-speaking countries.
According to the organization’s official announcement , the leaders are expected to discuss trade, transportation, energy and institutional cooperation, appoint a new secretary-general and adopt the Ankara Declaration.
Turkey and Azerbaijan maintain close military, energy and transportation ties and frequently describe their relationship as “one nation, two states.”

As coalition negotiations loom and allegations of foreign election interference emerge, Fox News Digital reporter Efrat Lachter reports from Tel Aviv, Israel.
Israel's final election count has confirmed that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc has lost its parliamentary majority, but whether opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot can assemble a government to replace him remains an open question as negotiations begin behind closed doors.
The completed count, published early Friday by Israel's Central Elections Committee , gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for Eisenkot's opposition alliance. The two predominantly Arab parties secured a historic 19 seats, placing them in a potentially decisive position.
Netanyahu's Likud emerged as the largest individual party with 27 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar with 21 and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett's Beyachad with 12. Final voter turnout reached 77.9%, according to the Central Elections Committee results .
ISRAEL HEADS INTO DEEPLY DIVIDED ELECTION AS OCT. 7 RECKONING LOOMS: WHAT TO KNOW

(Nir Keidar/Anadolu via Getty Images)
But the numbers leave neither major bloc with the 61 seats required for a majority, opening a complex political struggle involving potential partnerships with Arab parties, ultra-Orthodox lawmakers or a unity government bringing together longtime rivals.
A source familiar with opposition discussions, who spoke to Fox News Digital on condition of anonymity, described the outcome as a "bitter stalemate," but not an impossible political situation.
The source said opposition leaders are approaching coalition negotiations with patience and experience rather than treating the inconclusive results as a defeat, arguing that the next government could depend on their ability to forge partnerships that previously seemed unlikely.

An ultra-Orthodox Jewish man holds his ballot as he votes in the parliamentary election at a polling station in Jerusalem on January 22, 2013. Israelis voted on Tuesday in an election widely expected to win Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a third term in office, pushing the Jewish State further to the right, away from peace with Palestinians and towards a showdown with Iran. (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)
In a potentially significant development Friday, Israeli journalist Yishai Cohen of Kikar HaShabbat reported that Rabbi Dov Lando, a leading ultra-Orthodox religious authority, had instructed lawmakers from Degel HaTorah, part of United Torah Judaism, to open discussions with the opposition.
According to the report, the objective is to reach an arrangement protecting the status of yeshiva students amid the longstanding dispute over mandatory military service.
Channel 12 reported that figures within the ultra-Orthodox party were considering allowing an Eisenkot-led minority government to survive through outside parliamentary support, potentially breaking with Netanyahu.
"Our votes are not in Netanyahu's pocket," party figures told Channel 12, according to a translation of the Hebrew-language report.
However, the office of United Torah Judaism Chairman Yaakov Asher denied that any instruction to begin negotiations had been issued.
Such an arrangement would represent a significant shift from the party's longstanding alliance with Netanyahu. Eisenkot's pledge to expand military conscription among ultra-Orthodox men remains a major obstacle, although Channel 12 reported that party figures were willing to consider a compromise on the issue.
The source familiar with opposition discussions told Fox News Digital that Eisenkot's camp had been preparing for the possibility of cooperation with ultra-Orthodox parties well before the election, suggesting that some of the options now being discussed had already been under consideration behind the scenes.
According to the source, such an arrangement could require compromises over military service and potentially outside parliamentary support from Arab lawmakers, bringing together political factions whose positions appeared irreconcilable during the campaign.
FORMER ISRAELI PM EMERGES AS WILD CARD IN HIGH-STAKES ELECTION WITH MIDDLE EAST'S FUTURE AT STAKE
People gather near a pre-election campaign banner featuring leaders of the Joint List, ahead of Israel's national election, in Nazareth, Israel, on October 10, 2026. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)
Another possibility rests with the Arab parties, which nearly doubled their parliamentary representation from 10 to 19 seats following a surge in turnout.
But the prospects of an Arab-backed government have drawn conflicting assessments.
Channel 12 reported Thursday that Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas had expressed deep skepticism about the possibility of establishing an Eisenkot-led minority government supported by Arab lawmakers.
Israeli political commentator Amit Segal also argued that the available options had narrowed considerably, identifying a Netanyahu-Eisenkot unity government or another election as the two principal remaining possibilities.
Mohammed Majadla, head of the news division at Radio Nas and a Channel 12 political commentator, offered a different assessment in an interview with Fox News Digital, arguing that both Ra'am and the Joint List were prepared to use their parliamentary influence to prevent Netanyahu from returning to power.
"The two Arab lists agree on two things," Majadla said in the Hebrew-language interview. "First, they are prepared to do everything within the political process to ensure Netanyahu does not return to power."
According to Majadla, that could include joining a coalition, providing outside parliamentary support or abstaining from key votes.
He said their second shared priority was avoiding another election, which Arab political leaders fear could reverse their gains.
"The ball is now in Eisenkot's court, not in the Arab parties' court," Majadla said. "As far as the Arab parties are concerned, I can tell you they are truly prepared to do everything to make this happen."
Majadla suggested that public declarations should not necessarily be treated as final positions, particularly as parties seek leverage during coalition negotiations.
The difficulties extend beyond the Arab parties. Eisenkot's potential partners include politicians who strongly oppose cooperation with ultra-Orthodox factions, while several opposition leaders campaigned against relying on Arab lawmakers to govern.

articles.title_orig: Binance Suspends Transactions After It Is Targeted in Biggest-Ever Cyber Heist
articles.title_zh: Binance Suspends Transactions After It Is Targeted in Biggest-Ever Cyber Heist
articles.content_orig:
The digital currency exchange Binance says it was the target of a $6.3 billion crypto heist Thursday, believed to be the largest ever recorded.
The company has suspended all deposits and withdrawals while it works with law enforcement to secure its infrastructure and locate stolen funds.
The hack originated from a compromised laptop, it said, which allowed “an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.”
“The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said late Thursday on X .
About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said.
Binance will “cover all losses” from the hack, it said, adding, “User funds are safe.”
“We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice,” it said.
Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars’ worth of digital currencies on the exchange.
Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges.
The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025.
Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change.
“ This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets,” it said.
As word of the hack spread online Thursday, major cryptocurrencies traded lower. Bitcoin was down about 4.3%, while Ethereum lost 4.6% of its value.
Two major stablecoin issuers, Tether and Circle, said they had identified billions of dollars in assets connected to the hackers and had frozen them.
Tether froze more than $1.567 billion worth of its digital currency, CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X .
Jeremy Allaire, CEO of stablecoin issuer Circle, said the company had also frozen hundreds of millions of dollars of assets and was coordinating with law enforcement.
The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence.
Digital currency has been a primary target of hackers for years. In 2025, Coinbase disclosed that thieves had stolen customers’ personal information and tried to extort the company for $20 million . Coinbase refused to pay and offered a bounty for information leading to arrests, instead.
Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, “As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”
Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws. President Donald Trump later granted him a full pardon .
David Ingram is a tech reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Putin shuts down Russia’s last independent newspaper
articles.title_zh: Putin shuts down Russia’s last independent newspaper
articles.content_orig:
Emily covers breaking news from all over the world. She previously reported on home news and politics for The Telegraph. You can reach her at emily.smith@telegraph.co.uk
Vladimir Putin has shut down Russia’s last independent newspaper.
The Russian president has ordered the closure of Novaya Gazeta after 33 years. It had previously been placed on a list of state enemies.
The newspaper, which is known for its critical coverage of Russian political and social affairs, has been classed as a “foreign agent” by Moscow .
Sergei Sokolov, the paper’s editor-in-chief, said in a video statement on YouTube: “Novaya Gazeta is ceasing to exist. The Russian authorities, the Russian special services, have forced the editorial team to end its work.”
The paper was previously placed under investigation, with one of its journalists detained and the home of a senior editor searched.
Mr Sokolov added: “Novaya Gazeta has been killed... On Nov 9 we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave.
“They’re simply throwing us out, giving us barely any time to pack up. The Anna Politkovskaya museum is closing, and portraits of our friends who were killed are being taken down from the walls.”
Mr Sokolov was taken in for questioning earlier this month when his home was searched.
Novaya Gazeta was founded in 1993. It stopped publishing its print edition in 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine.
A European edition of the paper – Novaya Gazeta Europe – was launched from Latvia to avoid censorship, but the website was later blocked by Russia.
Shortly after the invasion, Russia’s Basmanny Court also revoked Novaya Gazeta’s media licence.
Novaya Gazeta’s office, located on Potapovsky Lane, also housed a museum in tribute to Anna Politkovskaya, one of the newspaper’s reporters, who was killed 20 years ago this month when she was shot in front of her apartment in Moscow.
Dmitry Muratov, the newspaper’s former editor and a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, was travelling to Paris on Oct 19 for a commemoration of her death when he discovered the publication was being evicted.
He and Mr Sokolov gathered the paper’s remaining staff on Oct 26 in the basement of the building next door because it was too dangerous to talk in the office, owing to a break-in the previous night.
Staff agreed that it was time to shut down the publication.
“We haven’t died, they’ve killed us – along with the constitution,” Mr Muratov told The Economist. “You can only laugh at Article 29 of the constitution: ‘Censorship is prohibited’.”
He said Novaya Gazeta “was our city”, adding: “They’ve destroyed this city and we’re leaving. But we are not leaving our work.”
A change to the Russian Criminal Code was passed in March 2022, eight days after the invasion of Ukraine, which criminalised the dissemination of “false information” about the Russian military.
Since the law was passed, at least 30 independent Russian media outlets have been forced to close.
Oleg Roldugin, a Novaya Gazeta journalist, was arrested in April and charged with “unlawful access to computerised information”. He pleaded not guilty, according to the state RIA news agency.

Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.

articles.title_orig: Volkswagen Will Take China-Developed Technology Global In Major Strategy Shift
articles.title_zh: Volkswagen Will Take China-Developed Technology Global In Major Strategy Shift
articles.content_orig:
Volkswagen is done keeping its Chinese software locked inside China. The automaker said its China Electronic Architecture (CEA), built with local electric vehicle maker Xpeng , will underpin next-generation models bound for South America and South Africa. That marks a sharp break from the brand's old "in China, for China" approach.
Now that same software stack is being lined up for Europe. A report summarized by Reuters says Volkswagen is studying whether the China Electronic Architecture could form the basis for future mass-market cars from its VW, Skoda, and Cupra brands in Europe, with the plan still under discussion inside the group.
As reported by Reuters , Volkswagen plans to integrate China-developed technology into South American product lineups starting in 2030 . Volkswagen Group China now uses the China Electronic Architecture in five locally produced all-electric Volkswagen brand models, including the Yuzhong 06 and Yuzhong 07.
Volkswagen Group China laid out the broader package, called VEGA, at a Technology Day event in Hefei. VEGA ties together the China Main Platform, the China Electronic Architecture, and China-developed software and driver-assistance systems into one scalable package for software-defined vehicles across multiple segments.
The China Main Platform targets A-segment battery-electric and plug-in-hybrid models. Volkswagen's stated goal is more than 373 miles of CLTC range and roughly 11 kWh per 62 miles in its most efficient version. Volkswagen says the China-built software could extend further still, with the Europe proposal covering roughly three quarters of the next-generation lineups for VW, Skoda, and Cupra .
Exports of China-developed vehicles are also starting to ramp up around 2026. China-built Volkswagens are already heading to markets such as Mexico and parts of Southeast and Central Asia, with more destinations planned afterward. That export push would run alongside the deeper platform integration planned for 2030.
The architecture trims the number of electronic control units by about 30 percent compared with Volkswagen's older setups. Volkswagen says that reduction is central to cutting development costs and complexity across its lineup.
It's a hardware play as much as a software one. Volkswagen intends to bring the same architecture to plug-in-hybrid and combustion models in China by 2027, which would widen its reach past the battery-electric vehicles where it currently lives and give future gas and hybrid products the same software backbone.
Looking further out, Volkswagen is targeting Level 4 automated driving by 2029, built on a third-generation version of the China Electronic Architecture paired with a Volkswagen-developed C7H control chip. That automated-driving target sits alongside the South America plan and the potential European rollout.
The strategy also threatens to sideline Rivian , Volkswagen's US software partner in a $5.8 billion investment central to CEO Oliver Blume's technology plans. A separate report from German outlet Manager Magazin said core brand chief Thomas Schäfer is weighing a proposal to use China-developed software as the basis for future Volkswagen, Skoda, and Cupra models, which would leave Rivian focused on other group brands even if the joint venture itself stays in place.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu bloc short of majority as Arab parties secure record seats
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu bloc short of majority as Arab parties secure record seats
articles.content_orig:
Final results from Israel's pivotal legislative election this week showed there was no clear winner, with both of the two main blocs well short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc finished on 53 seats, while the opposition camp, led by the centrist Yashar party of rival Gadi Eisenkot, ended on 48.
Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party remained the largest party, with 27 seats, while the Arab parties secured a record 19 seats between them.
The result means Israel is now set to face a lengthy and likely tricky period of negotiations as party leaders work to form a government. Failure to do so would see Israelis head back to the polls.
Netanyahu has accused Arab parties of "stealing" the election, calling on police and Israel's domestic security service Shin Bet to carry out a "thorough investigation into election fraud."
The Likud party also pushed claims that foreign funding had been used to influence voters in the election. The allegations focused on claims that the Ra'am party had received money from Qatar.
"The ‘Ra’am-gate’ scandal is an earthquake. The Israeli elections have been stolen," Likud said in a statement on Thursday.
Ra'am party leader Mansour Abbas reportedly denied any wrongdoing and said he would welcome an investigation.
In a post on social media, Eisenkot said foreign interference was "unacceptable and extremely serious" and called on Shin Bet to investigate the allegations "fully and immediately, without bias."
Moving forward, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will consult with leaders of the parties elected to the Knesset before assigning the task of trying to form a government to the candidate he believes has the best chance of securing sufficient support to do so.
Under Israeli law, that individual will have 28 days to carry out the job. The president is able to extend this by a maximum of 14 days if necessary.
Should that fail, the president can give a second leader the chance to form a government, this time with a maximum deadline of 28 days. If this second round were also to fail, then the Knesset can request a third candidate be given a go. They would have 14 days to complete the task.
If all attempts fail, another election is called.

articles.title_orig: Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Hacked in Crypto's Biggest Heist
articles.title_zh: Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Hacked in Crypto's Biggest Heist
articles.content_orig:
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has said that about $6.3bn in funds have been stolen in a “security incident” that looks to be the biggest crypto heist in history.
The world’s largest crypto exchange said on Thursday that it had suspended all deposits and withdrawals and that about $3bn in funds had been frozen following the apparent hacking.
Binance said an initial investigation suggested that a hacker had been able to make unauthorised transactions after gaining access to an engineer’s compromised laptop.
The company said it would cover all losses, adding that user funds were “safe”.
“Our teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly,” Binance said in a statement to Al Jazeera.
“We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice.”
The company added that it would share a “detailed” technical post-mortem once investigations were complete.
Changpeng Zhao, Binance’s founder and largest shareholder, said earlier that the exchange appeared to have been hacked.
TRM, a blockchain intelligence firm, said in a report that it assessed with “high confidence” that the attack was carried out by North Korea’s hacking unit TraderTraitor, which investigators have linked to the Lazarus Group.
Ari Redbord, TRM’s global head of policy, described the attack as “unprecedented” and a “watershed”.
“When North Korea steals at this scale, the money funds weapons proliferation and other destabilising activity. That makes this a global security issue, not just a crypto theft,” Redbord told Al Jazeera.
The price of Bitcoin, the world’s most popular cryptocurrency, fell about 5 percent following the heist, dropping below $77,000.
“Binance is one of the largest centralised exchanges, and so a blow to confidence in them risks shocking confidence to many retail investors, which could dampen prices of crypto assets,” Sean Foley, an expert in crypto markets at Macquarie University in Sydney, told Al Jazeera.
Foley said the attack highlighted the risks of centralised exchanges and could spur more traders to use decentralised alternatives.
“Any assets held at a centralised exchange are only as safe as the exchange itself, and the larger the exchange’s holdings, the larger a target it becomes,” Foley said.
The Binance hacking dwarfs the previous record for a crypto theft, set in 2025 when North Korean state-backed Lazarus Group carried out a $1.5bn heist on Bybit.
Cybercriminals stole $2.87bn in crypto assets in nearly 150 hacking incidents in 2025, according to the 2026 Crypto Crime Report produced by TRM.
Binance, founded in China by Zhao in 2017, has about $155bn in assets under management, more than any other exchange, according to CoinMarketCap.

By Iain Withers and Ankur Banerjee
LONDON/SINGAPORE, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Tech shares slumped on Friday and US bonds surged toward their biggest monthly gain in nearly three years, as investors scurried to safety due to worries that huge and rising AI spending may not deliver ‌sufficient returns.
Futures trading pointed to falls on Wall Street later in the session, including a more than 2% drop in the tech-heavy Nasdaq ‌100. That came alongside an out-of-hours plunge of 23% in Intel shares and a drop of 7% in Amazon as their results showed they burned through cash.
Shares in Google parent Alphabet fell 12.6% on ​Wall Street on Thursday and slid a little further after hours, to wipe out a stunning $500 billion in market value, as massive AI spending turned the company's cash flow negative.
European stocks opened down 0.2% on Friday, as the relative lack of big tech stocks helped limit losses. There were falls earlier in Asia led by chipmakers.
Investors are worried about the returns they can expect to make on the massive capital spending needed for the AI buildout and what effect it could have on consumers if ‌price hikes squeeze global demand for devices like smartphones ⁠and PCs. Anthropic's potentially record-breaking IPO could prove the next big test of sentiment.
"The next key milestone will be the Anthropic IPO, to see how that lands. If it's a poor listing, I think that could signal a bit of ⁠weakness going forward," said Jason Da Silva, co-chief investment officer at Arbuthnot Latham.
Nerves were also frayed by a potentially record-breaking hack at Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, which drove down bitcoin and other cryptocurrency prices.
The world's biggest cryptocurrency, bitcoin, hit a six-week low before cutting losses to trade 1.1% lower at $77,876.
"I suspect the negative price action still ​has ​some way to go," said Geoffrey Kendrick, head of digital assets research at Standard ​Chartered. "Only after assets are unfrozen and more detail of the ‌hack emerges will we find a new base."
In commodities, oil prices rose about 2% on Friday and were poised for a fourth monthly gain, as an attack on a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz waterway highlighted continuing supply risks from the US-Israeli war on Iran. [O/R]
The Bank of Japan left interest rates on hold, which was expected and did not trigger major currency or bond moves, although in a surprise development the central bank unveiled plans to sharply accelerate exchange-traded fund sales next year.
"While this may initially spook markets, I actually think this is a positive development since the BOJ feels confident ‌enough with the economy and market," said David Chao, global market strategist for Asia-Pacific at ​Invesco.
The central bank declared victory in a nearly 14-year battle to hit its price target and ​signalled vigilance against inflation risks, suggesting the next rate hike could ​come as soon as December.
Tech sector jitters have helped push a rush to bonds, further spurred by the Federal Reserve's ‌decision on Wednesday to keep US interest rates on hold, with ​no firm projection of when it might ​hike next.
Benchmark 10-year US Treasury yields fell around 7 basis points on Friday to 4.92% and were on track for their largest one-month drop since December 2023. Yields fall when bond prices rise.
The risk-averse mood strengthened haven currencies such as the yen and Swiss franc, with the ​yen slightly higher at 157.30 per dollar and the ‌franc at 0.821 to the dollar and not far from a one-month high.
The euro inched up 0.1% to $1.1194 but was set for ​a drop of over 1% in October, its second straight monthly decline.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, center left and Zhang Shengmin, Vice Chairman of the Central Military Commission second from right attend a ceremony in honor of fallen national heroes at the Monument to the People's Heroes to mark Martyrs' Day at Tiananmen Square in Beijing, Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Ng Han Guan/AP hide caption
BANGKOK — China's top leaders on Thursday elevated the only remaining general on the commission that oversees the country's military to the Politburo, the top governing body of the Communist Party.
The leaders also adopted a resolution on strengthening self-governance, discipline and anti-corruption in the party, as they seek to extend their grip on power.
During a four-day closed-door meeting, top Communist Party leaders deliberated on and adopted resolutions that will guide the party in the coming years. The meeting comes about a year before President Xi Jinping is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party's leader.
The party elected Gen. Zhang Shengmin, who currently serves as vice chairman of the Central Military Commission, to the Politburo. Xi had earlier purged two of China's top generals, leaving Zhang as the commission's only member besides Xi himself. It also left the Politburo without any representatives from the People's Liberation Army.
Zhang also holds a position overseeing internal discipline for the military, serving as deputy secretary of the CMC Commission for Discipline Inspection.
The party said in a summary of the resolution that the tasks facing it were "increasingly arduous," such as "uniting and leading the people to safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests."
It said it must step up its self-governance, which involves rooting out corruption and maintaining ideological purity.
The party should, "with an eye on enhancing its long-term governance capacity, maintain its progressive nature and purity, and its close, flesh-and-blood ties with the people," according to a summary of the resolution from the official Xinhua News Agency.
Xi has championed anti-corruption since coming to power in 2012, and has sustained a crackdown on officials for more than a decade. However, analysts say the focus now also includes underperforming officials.
Party members also reviewed the earlier purges of top members and military officials, confirming the personnel changes.
The plenum meeting revealed wider-than-expected purges, according to analysis by Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at Asia Policy who studies Chinese politics. He calculated an attendance rate of 74 percent, the lowest since the times of former leader Mao Zedong, who ran political purges regularly.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu alleges stolen election as he seeks political survival amid uncertainty
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu alleges stolen election as he seeks political survival amid uncertainty
articles.content_orig:
Danny Danon joins 'Fox & Friends First' to discuss Israel holding its first election since the October 7 attacks. He analyzes the future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and reacts to President Donald Trump's call for Netanyahu's re-election.
TEL AVIV, Israel: Israel's two Arab parties are in a position to have a say in who the country's next prime minister and government will be — but not if Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has anything to do with it, after he alleged serious criminal activities took place during voting in the Arab areas of the nation.
The two parties were projected to win a combined 19 Knesset seats, according to preliminary results. However, both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud-led right-wing bloc and the opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s centrist bloc fell short of the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
On Wednesday, Prime Minister Netanyahu wrote on X that Israel’s election had been "stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state," alleging serious criminal offenses, including bribery, threats, violence, forgery and the use of prohibited software to mobilize voters.
NETANYAHU GAINS OVERNIGHT AS ISRAEL ELECTION HEADS TOWARD POLITICAL DEADLOCK
People cast their votes at a polling station during Israel's legislative election in the Arab town of Taibe in northern Israel on Oct. 27, 2026. (Gil Cohen-Magen/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Images)
"The Likud party is transferring to the police, the Shin Bet and the Central Elections Committee hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence regarding election theft in many Arab polling stations," he wrote.
He cited allegations of thousands of envelopes containing cash and Ra’am ballot slips, threats and violence against polling station staff, multiple votes cast behind the voting curtain, voting under multiple identities, discrepancies between the number of ballot envelopes and the number of voters, the use of prohibited voter-mobilization software and other offenses.
"We demand from the police and the Shin Bet a thorough investigation into the election theft by the Arab parties and the full prosecution of the criminals. We demand from the Central Elections Committee an immediate response to investigate these criminal offenses that have severely damaged the integrity of the elections in Israel and the election results," he added.
In a letter addressed to Yesh Atid lawmaker Vladimir Beliak, Acting Central Elections Committee Director-General Dean Livne wrote that the elections "were conducted lawfully" and that, "to the best of my knowledge, there is no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity," the Times of Israel reported . He also acknowledged that the request for an investigation concerned classified information whose veracity had not yet been determined.
A boy sits on his bicycle next to a campaign banner of Netanyahu's Likud Party, ahead of the Israeli parliamentary election, in Bnei Brak, Israel, October 25, 2026. (Nir Elias/Reuters)
The political makeup of the Arab parties includes the Joint List, which brings together three parties: Hadash, a predominantly Arab-Jewish left-wing party rooted in Israel’s communist movement, and the Arab nationalist parties Ta’al and Balad. With over 90% of ballots counted, the alliance was projected to win 12 seats.
The other Arab party, the United Arab List (Ra’am), led by Mansour Abbas and affiliated with the Southern Branch of the Islamic Movement in Israel, was projected to win seven seats.
Arab citizens make up approximately 21% of Israel’s population. Turnout in this election reached a near record high of between 75% and 80%.
"They are a political force to be reckoned with," Dahlia Scheindlin, a former policy fellow at the Mitvim Institute and a senior analyst at Haaretz, told Fox News Digital.
NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reacts after filling out his ballot before voting at a polling station in Jerusalem on Oct. 27, 2026, on the day of Israel's legislative election. (Yonatan Sindel/Pool via Reuters)
Scheindlin said that Netanyahu framed his campaign around the claim that the opposition is prepared to form a government dependent on Arab parties’ support, which he argues would lead to the establishment of a Palestinian state that would become a terror state and ultimately bring about Israel’s destruction.
"This is the most consistent message, and he never stopped saying it, including on election day," she said.
Scheindlin said that the issue had become politically sensitive, prompting leading Zionist opposition parties to pledge not to cooperate with the Arab parties.
"They have sworn they would not build a coalition that depends on Arab votes, either from within the coalition or from outside it. If they receive any help, they will have to break that promise," she added.
It is not inconceivable, though highly unlikely, that Netanyahu could reach out to one of the Arab parties to explore the possibility of cooperation , Scheindlin said.
People gather near a pre-election campaign banner featuring leaders of the Joint List, ahead of Israel's national election, in Nazareth, Israel, Oct. 10, 2026. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)
ISRAEL HEADS INTO DEEPLY DIVIDED ELECTION AS OCT. 7 RECKONING LOOMS: WHAT TO KNOW
Dr. Arik Rudnitzky, a researcher in the Israel Democracy Institute’s Arab Society in Israel Program, said that Arab parties had historically remained in the opposition and had not joined governing coalitions.
During the governments of Yitzhak Rabin and, later, Shimon Peres in the 1990s, Arab parties provided a parliamentary safety net from outside the coalition. This enabled the government to remain in office and complete its term even after it effectively became a minority government amid opposition to the Oslo Accords , as the Haredi Shas Party left the government.
"Historically, Arab parties were always in the opposition for many reasons. It was quite uncommon to believe Arab parties could [support] the government. It’s a novelty of recent years, plus the fact that their political strength in terms of the number of seats was not as significant as it is today," Rudnitzky said.
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar ("Straight") Party, waves an Israeli flag onstage following the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election in Tel Aviv, Israel, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (Ariel Schalit/AP Photo)
Demographic changes alone do not explain the Arab parties’ growing political strength, Rudnitzky said; shifting voting patterns have also played a role.
"In the past, Arab voters supported both Arab and Jewish parties. In the 1980s and 1990s, approximately half voted for Jewish parties," he continued.
Rudnitzky said historical developments, the impact of the Oslo Accords and the entry of new Arab representatives into the Knesset contributed to a gradual shift away from Jewish parties, with more Arab voters turning to Arab parties.
"Today, we can say that between 85% and 90% of Arab voters support Arab parties. This is the main reason for their increased political strength," he added.
Any support Arab parties might provide to a prospective coalition would come in exchange for political concessions, Rudnitzky said. Their demands would likely include a government decision and a plan to combat crime in Arab communities, as well as a new socioeconomic development plan for the Arab sector involving budget allocations.
Ultimately, he said, such arrangements would involve allocating public goods and resources in exchange for political support. "There is no free lunch in politics. Every collaboration, either within a coalition or from the outside, has its political price."

articles.content_orig:
In brief: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in Atlanta on Friday, Oct. 30 for the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting despite objections from US lawmakers and European allies. Moscow plans to challenge Western sanctions as Washington prepares new peace talks involving Ukraine and Russia.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in the US on Friday, Oct. 30, for a G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, despite calls from US lawmakers to bar him from the country while Moscow continues its war and deadly attacks on Ukrainian civilians.
Lavrov’s arrival, reported by Russia’s state-owned TASS news agency, comes days after Russian strikes killed civilians across Ukraine, including 14 people at a railway station in Dnipro.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The Kremlin’s top diplomat, under US sanctions since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, is expected to use the Oct. 30-31 gathering to criticize Western sanctions against Moscow, according to Russia’s Foreign Ministry.
Republican Rep. Don Bacon sharply condemned Lavrov’s visit, calling for the Russian foreign minister to be barred from entering the US while Moscow continues its deadly attacks on Ukrainian cities.
“Lavrov should not be allowed in the country. As long as Putin is waging war against Ukraine and bombing cities, Russian leaders should not be welcomed in any of these forums. They lead a pariah state,” Bacon wrote on X on Wednesday, Oct. 28.
Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, also sharply criticized Trump’s approach to Moscow, demanding that Washington stop extending diplomatic legitimacy to Putin’s regime while Russian forces continue killing Ukrainian civilians.
“Donald Trump needs to wake up,” Shaheen said in an Oct. 8 CNN interview. “He needs to understand that courting favor with Vladimir Putin is not good for America.”
Shaheen, who joined 13 bipartisan senators in calling for Putin and other sanctioned Russian officials to be barred from G20 events on US soil, urged the administration to increase pressure on Moscow rather than reward it with international recognition.
In their letter to Trump , the senators questioned why Russia should receive diplomatic legitimacy while continuing its deadly attacks on Ukraine’s cities and civilian infrastructure.
The bipartisan criticism comes just days before the Nov. 3 US midterm elections, with the Trump administration facing questions over its approach to Moscow amid continued Russian strikes on Ukraine.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Lavrov would use his appearance to argue against economic sanctions and other trade restrictions, portraying them as instruments of pressure.
The Russian delegation also intends to promote Moscow’s vision of a multipolar international order.
The visit comes as Washington prepares new trilateral talks involving the US, Ukraine, and Russia, expected in November in Abu Dhabi.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is hosting the G20 gathering, which will address major international disputes alongside energy security, trade and global supply chains.
The meeting also precedes the Dec. 14-15 G20 leaders’ summit at President Trump’s Doral resort in Miami, to which Putin has been invited. His attendance remains unconfirmed.
According to the State Department’s delegation list, Lavrov is attending alongside foreign ministers from major NATO and European countries, including Germany’s Johann Wadephul, France’s Jean-Noël Barrot, Poland’s Radosław Sikorski, Canada’s Anita Anand, and Turkey’s Hakan Fidan.
Other participants include EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, Britain’s Ed Miliband, Australia’s Penny Wong, India’s Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, and Japan’s Toshimitsu Motegi.
China is represented by Executive Vice Foreign Minister Ma Zhaoxu rather than Foreign Minister Wang Yi.
Ukraine was not invited, although it had participated in previous G20 meetings as a guest. US officials said the decision reflected a policy of limiting invitations to formal members. South Africa was also excluded amid tensions with Washington.
Russia’s participation has unsettled some Western allies, who have questioned the invitation while Moscow intensifies its attacks on Ukraine.
The G20 meeting opens as Washington seeks renewed diplomatic engagement with Moscow, while Ukraine and its European partners continue pressing for stronger sanctions and security guarantees.

articles.title_zh: Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history
articles.content_orig:
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record.
The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses".
Early checks show the incident may have involved an engineer's laptop that had been compromised, which allowed an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said.
Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor.
Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack.
Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record".
AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen.
The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack.
For the last few years North Korea-linked operatives have focussed on attacking cryptocurrency companies for large thefts of digital tokens.
Western security agencies have previously said stolen funds are used to finance North Korea's nuclear weapons and missile development programs.
The regime has denied any involvement in hacks in the past.
Eric Jardine, Chainalysis' Head of Research, urged every exchange to remain vigilant as the platforms are attractive targets for hackers due to the sheer value of assets.
Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."
The incident concerns Binance.com - while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US, which provides trading services specifically for American residents - said its platform is not affected by the issue.
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the company's initial investigation suggested the hack started with a compromised engineer's laptop.
"That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions," he said in a statement.
"To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual. So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak."
He said a detailed "post-mortem" would be shared once the investigation was complete.
Check Point's Dave said this attack also resembled a hack on crypto exchange platform Bitget in September in which $388m (£289m) was lost: "This implies that attackers no longer need the vault keys. They target the systems and people with authority to use them."
In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets.
"Safety first: withdrawals are currently disabled until the environment is confirmed to be secure," she said.
Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack.
World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it has worked with its partners to freeze stolen funds.
Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation.
Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue.
Bitcoin dropped by more than 4% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.

articles.title_zh: Blockchain analysis firm TRM says North Korea behind Binance crypto theft
articles.content_orig:
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has said that about $6.3bn in funds have been stolen in a “security incident” that looks to be the biggest crypto heist in history.
The world’s largest crypto exchange said on Thursday that it had suspended all deposits and withdrawals and that about $3bn in funds had been frozen following the apparent hacking.
Binance said an initial investigation suggested that a hacker had been able to make unauthorised transactions after gaining access to an engineer’s compromised laptop.
The company said it would cover all losses, adding that user funds were “safe”.
“Our teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly,” Binance said in a statement to Al Jazeera.
“We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice.”
The company added that it would share a “detailed” technical post-mortem once investigations were complete.
Changpeng Zhao, Binance’s founder and largest shareholder, said earlier that the exchange appeared to have been hacked.
TRM, a blockchain intelligence firm, said in a report that it assessed with “high confidence” that the attack was carried out by North Korea’s hacking unit TraderTraitor, which investigators have linked to the Lazarus Group.
Ari Redbord, TRM’s global head of policy, described the attack as “unprecedented” and a “watershed”.
“When North Korea steals at this scale, the money funds weapons proliferation and other destabilising activity. That makes this a global security issue, not just a crypto theft,” Redbord told Al Jazeera.
The price of Bitcoin, the world’s most popular cryptocurrency, fell about 5 percent following the heist, dropping below $77,000.
“Binance is one of the largest centralised exchanges, and so a blow to confidence in them risks shocking confidence to many retail investors, which could dampen prices of crypto assets,” Sean Foley, an expert in crypto markets at Macquarie University in Sydney, told Al Jazeera.
Foley said the attack highlighted the risks of centralised exchanges and could spur more traders to use decentralised alternatives.
“Any assets held at a centralised exchange are only as safe as the exchange itself, and the larger the exchange’s holdings, the larger a target it becomes,” Foley said.
The Binance hacking dwarfs the previous record for a crypto theft, set in 2025 when North Korean state-backed Lazarus Group carried out a $1.5bn heist on Bybit.
Cybercriminals stole $2.87bn in crypto assets in nearly 150 hacking incidents in 2025, according to the 2026 Crypto Crime Report produced by TRM.
Binance, founded in China by Zhao in 2017, has about $155bn in assets under management, more than any other exchange, according to CoinMarketCap.

articles.title_zh: Carney, top EU official push Canada associate membership and wider alliance against Trump threats
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is hosting European Union leaders in Montreal on Friday as he looks to deepen ties with like-minded leaders in the face of an increasingly protectionist United States.
But the rise of nationalist political forces in Europe could make that more difficult in the years to come.
The 21st Canada-EU summit, which wraps Friday, is aimed at forging a stronger alliance between Canada and the 27-member bloc in the face of an unpredictable and volatile White House.
On Thursday, both Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stressed the two sides' shared values as they pitched an "alliance for the future" based on deeper trade and security ties.
Carney says Canada is working to become an 'associate member' as he hosts EU leaders in Montreal
EU dropping associate membership title for its closer alliance with Canada
But shifting political winds on the continent could test that alliance, notably in France and Germany — heavyweights within the bloc.
In France, presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally is leading in polls ahead of the spring 2027 election. Le Pen, an advocate for strict immigration limits, has criticized the EU-Canada trade pact.
While in Germany, the far-right and isolationist Alternative for Germany (AfD) continues to gain ground in regional parliaments and national polls.
Asked Thursday if he has concerns about dealing with a potentially different political makeup, Carney praised the EU's adherence to democratic values.
Canada forging 'alliance for the future' with EU as an 'associate member,' Carney says
"One of Europe's strengths is democracy, freedom and a core belief in the rule of law. There will always be different governments, governments of different stripes in Europe," he told reporters.
"Over the course of decades, the European Union has continued to develop, and strengthen, throughout, and be enriched by the national democratic processes of those countries."
Carney also downplayed the notion he was looking to secure commitments with the EU before the French election.
"We're not tying it to any political cycle, but to the fundamentals of what they deliver … for Canadians," he said.
Far right gains ground in Europe as Canada pivots from Trump to EU
Despite some objections from EU members, von der Leyen has pitched making Canada the first associate member of the bloc. Carney has welcomed a more expansive alliance across the Atlantic.
That appeared to anger U.S. President Donald Trump who said if he interpreted the move as a "hostile act," he might stop trading with Europe "on many things."
Asked earlier this week about the summit potentially attracting retaliation from Trump or right-wing leaders in Europe, a senior Canadian government official told reporters the gathering isn't directed against anyone but reflected deep interests between Canada and the EU.
As the two-day summit winds down, the Canadian and European sides are expected to release a joint statement on Friday with a number of new commitments.
A draft version of the statement seen by CBC News commits to reinforcing "a predictable trade environment," deepening collaboration in critical mineral supply chains, countering cyberattacks and continued support for Ukraine.
Both sides are also promising to launch negotiations toward deeper participation in Erasmus, the European Union's student and youth exchange program.

articles.title_zh: Chinese Embassy in Mexico slams US officials’ malicious smears against China-Mexico cooperation
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — A top aide to U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said in a phone call Monday night that prosecutors had made a “f---up” in a high-profile criminal case against two former FBI officials , an agent who’s been investigating the case testified Thursday.
The former officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, were initially charged last week with making false statements to Congress about their level of knowledge about an investigation of Hunter Biden’s laptop.
A sworn affidavit attached to the complaint by Special Agent Ryan Witt cited a congressional staffer who was present for both Floris’ and Benavides’ testimony — but it turns out the person was only present for Benavides’, Witt testified at a preliminary hearing on whether there’s probable cause to charge the pair.
Witt told Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui that he called the congressional staffer on Monday and was later joined on the call by Pirro aide Carlton Davis and Pirro, the top federal prosecutor for Washington, D.C.
Audio of that conversation was turned over to Benavides’ attorney, Ron Safer, who read parts of the exchange in court and asked Witt whether it was accurate.
At one point, Davis told the staffer, House Judiciary Committee general counsel Steve Castor, “This is our f---up,” and asked for his help finding someone who had been present for the testimony, Witt confirmed.
Witt added that he still has not been able to speak to anyone who was there.
Later Monday night, prosecutors filed what they called a superseding criminal complaint and a new affidavit, neither of which was signed by any law enforcement officer or judge. Faruqui tossed the complaint on Tuesday.
On Wednesday, one of the attorneys for the defense asked Witt if it was unusual for a case alleging defendants made false statements to use an affidavit containing false statements — a question the judge cut off.
Davis, who is listed as a special counsel in Pirro’s office, was involved in the failed effort to indict six sitting members of Congress over their comments in a social media video where they urged members of the military not to follow illegal orders. Davis previously worked as a Republican staffer on several committees, including the House Select Committee on Benghazi.
Witt was on the stand in the case for a third day.
He testified Tuesday that he was assigned to the case in July after FBI Director Kash Patel sent a letter directing the Kansas City, Missouri, office to look into certain people, including Floris.
The direction came a day after President Donald Trump delivered an Oval Office address in which he complained that “rogue bureaucrats” had suppressed information about China’s efforts to interfere in the 2020 election, which he falsely claims was “stolen.”
Both Floris and Benavides were involved in FBI efforts to secure the election and have long been targets of criticism from Trump’s allies.
Witt said he was unhappy with the assignment, in part because “I had concerns that this would be viewed as political.”
Witt said Wednesday that top FBI brass, including Patel, had been checking on progress in the case through in-person meetings, videoconferences and updates pushed through their special agent in charge. Witt said both FBI deputy directors — Chris Raia and Andrew Bailey, who recently resigned — were involved.
“The evidence in this case speaks for itself [as] to the effect that kind of pressure has on sensitive investigations like this one,” Floris’ attorney Mary Dohrmann told the judge Thursday.
She said there were other mistakes in the affidavit as well, and that some of the false statements her client was alleged to have made were presented stripped of necessary context.
Safer, Benavides’ attorney, told Faruqui that in most instances, calling something a political prosecution is a talking point, but not in this case.
“That is the price we pay to allow politics to infect the process,” he said.
The judge said he plans to issue a written ruling Monday morning.
Ryan J. Reilly is a justice reporter for NBC News.
Tanish Bijur is an intern on the Justice and National Security Unit
Dareh Gregorian is a politics reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Canada and Europe share challenge of diversifying without antagonizing US and China
articles.title_zh: Canada and Europe share challenge of diversifying without antagonizing US and China
articles.content_orig:
MONTREAL — There’s one thing the European Union and Canada want to avoid with their new alliance: stoking new fury from Washington and Beijing.
Officials have been under pressure to check off everything they said they would do at the last summit and on Friday will unveil the areas they plan to focus on over the next year, as they intensify their transatlantic cooperation. But don’t expect a parade of new deals.
“Canada has objectives where they need our technology — so you can build a beautiful relationship if you focus on it,” one senior EU official told POLITICO about shared challenges in diversifying away from the U.S. and China. The official was granted anonymity to speak candidly about sensitive diplomatic negotiations between Brussels and Ottawa.
One of the core EU interests in Canada, the official explained, is a chance for the bloc to diversify its supply of critical raw materials and sources of energy to further reduce its dependence on China and Russia, respectively.
“They have most of what we need,” the official said about Canadian minerals. “There’s also a huge opportunity to bring Canadian fossil fuels and gas to the EU.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed the controversy over whether the EU should label the relationship with Canada as an “associate membership,” saying on Thursday it was a sideshow to what’s been billed as a landmark summit.
Earlier this week, Germany, France, Greece and other countries opposed the definition in a joint EU-Canada statement to be issued in Montreal. That came after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen put forward the “associate membership” label in September.
But Carney told reporters on Thursday that the new alliance wasn’t “a marketing exercise” and that the name doesn’t matter. “What matters is that the complementarities of our two jurisdictions strengthen our sovereignty, strengthen Europe’s sovereignty, various strategic autonomies, critical minerals, energy, other aspects — AI,” he said.
A tricky political road lies ahead as Carney and von der Leyen make moves to draw the EU and Canada closer in a partnership that doesn’t include its southern neighbor. They’ll need to  tiptoe forward with an “association without accession” work plan in the last years of the U.S. President Donald Trump’s time in office.
Montreal’s historic Fairmont The Queen Elizabeth hotel was a hub of summit activity on Thursday, beginning with a morning spectacle of von der Leyen heading out of the hotel in runners, taking staff out for a walking meeting. EU commissioners and Canadian Cabinet ministers sailed in and out of the hotel’s perfumed lobby, greeting colleagues.
Jet-lagged Europeans, along with Canadian officials and lobbyists, commiserated over what they saw as poor summit organization, spread across multiple locations.
The debate over membership semantics became a luncheon laugh line when European Council President António Costa endorsed Von der Leyen’s offer to Canada before joking the final designation is “subject to revision”
Then, between servings of frisée salad and roast salmon, Costa struck a diplomatic balance.
“Tomorrow, the European Union and Canada will launch an alliance for the future of Europe,” he said, invoking German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s preferred label and a term Carney has also used to describe the relationship. But Costa also backed von der Leyen’s “ambition” of Canada as an “associate member” of the EU, admitting the term might not matter in the end.
By mid-afternoon, Carney seemed to come around to the term, recognizing the work underway to deepen relations as “an alliance for the future, with Canada as an associate member, between Canada and the European Union.”
The two sides are expected to announce a wrap on talks on a new digital trade agreement on Friday, ending negotiations that were launched in the spring. Other anticipated outcomes include an agreement between the European Investment Bank and Canada, geared to allow the bloc to fund Canadian critical minerals projects.
Eleven EU commissioners in town to “further an agenda” is no small accomplishment, Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne told reporters. “It’s a historic moment that we need to seize.”
AI and energy companies are expected to be major beneficiaries of an enhanced EU–Canada relationship, making the absences of European Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen and Canadian Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson noteworthy.
Zoya Sheftalovich contributed to this report from Montreal.
